sessions.title: AIDP: possible sale within two years
sessions.to_check: Who said AIDP will be for sale (the note does not say); the currency of the revenue figure (US revenue, so probably dollars); who owns AIDP and ThreoTech now.
sessions.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's note, 17 Nov 2026)
sessions.notes:
Nathan's note from day 1 of FiE, 17 Nov 2026, dictated, verbatim (the part about this company; his opening line first):

Quick note from the first day of FIE I've been speaking to lots of people about things and all of the big takeaways are three specific companies that either are out for sale or will be up for sale in the next 2 to 3 years.

Also AIDP will be up for sale in the next two years, they are a massive company with over 100 million in US revenue, probably a bit too big for us but could be a fantastic acquisition for us or someone else.

summary.Summary:
On the first day of FiE, Nathan heard that AIDP will be up for sale within the next two years. He called it a massive company with over 100 million in US revenue: probably too big for Vita Actives alone, but a fantastic acquisition for us or someone else. His note does not say who told him.

AIDP is a privately held US ingredient company in City of Industry, California, founded in 1996 by Edward Lee. Lee died unexpectedly; his death was announced in March 2026. Jennifer Gu, his partner and head of research since the start, is now chief executive. A founder's sudden death is a common reason for a sale.

Its main owned asset is Magtein, magnesium L-threonate, with US GRAS status and EU and UK novel food authorisations that carry five years of data protection. Since 2024 a separate company, ThreoTech, has run Magtein, so a buyer of AIDP alone might not get it. AIDP also owns prebiotic GOS technology bought from France's Olygose in 2020, and distributes about 40 partner brands, among them collagen, plant protein and botanicals.

No accounts are public. AIDP says it has more than 60 staff, and public revenue estimates run from 6.9 million to 100 million dollars, below Nathan's figure. It has no European office.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Nathan was told AIDP will be up for sale within the next two years; who said it is not recorded (notes).
- Nathan's view: "probably a bit too big for us but could be a fantastic acquisition for us or someone else" (notes).
- Size differs by source: Nathan heard over 100 million in US revenue (notes); public estimates are 25 to 100 million dollars (Owler) and 6.9 million dollars (ZoomInfo), and AIDP says it has more than 60 staff. No filed accounts were found. My reading: the figure Nathan heard is the one to test first.
- My reading: the founder's death, announced in March 2026, is a likely trigger for a sale; no adviser or sale process is public.
- My reading: Magtein is the prize, and its ownership is split. AIDP holds the EU data rights, ThreoTech (separate since 2024) runs the brand, the patent licence and its staff.
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: one of three companies Nathan named at FiE as for sale or soon to be (notes).
- My reading: Magtein is the magnesium form that still holds a price premium in Europe while other forms compete on price, on Nick Stene's third slide at the Healthspan Summit (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). A form with a premium and EU exclusivity to November 2029 is worth more than a commodity range.
- My reading: AIDP's range overlaps ours in healthy ageing, collagen and plant protein, with little in creatine or core sports.
- My reading: much of the range is partner brands held on distribution contracts, which may not survive a change of owner; a buyer would need to know which brands AIDP owns outright.
- My reading: if a purchase is too big, a European route for Magtein or for AIDP's US partner brands is a smaller way in, since AIDP has no European entity.

summary.Research:
Desk research on public sources, 17 Nov 2026. Nothing Nathan was told went into a search.
- Identity: AIDP, Inc. ("Advanced Ingredients for Dietary Products"), 19535 East Walnut Drive South, City of Industry, CA; founded 1996 by Edward Lee, PhD; started in commodity trading and moved to clinically backed branded ingredients in the mid-2000s.
- Leadership: Lee's death was announced on 2 to 3 March 2026 and described as unexpected. Jennifer Gu, PhD, his "lifelong partner" and head of R&D since the start, became CEO of AIDP and ThreoTech and took his board seats. President: Mark Thurston. Ownership is not stated anywhere public.
- Magtein (magnesium L-threonate): US GRAS since 2012; EU novel food from 7 Nov 2024 with five years of data exclusivity (Regulation 2024/2694), held by AIDP with ThreoTech as licensee; UK novel food authorised March 2026 with five years of data protection; in "over 400 products"; a 33% five-year US growth rate and sold through Walmart, Target and Costco (ThreoTech, April 2025). Patents trace to Magceutics (an MIT and Tsinghua discovery). Two Vitafoods 2026 awards.
- ThreoTech, LLC: the "standalone" Magtein company, created April 2024 by one account and spun off in 2025 by another; its ownership is not disclosed.
- Prebiotics: bought Olygose SAS's core technology and IP in October 2020 (AlphaGOS, pea GOS, a soluble pea protein process; 16 patents claimed); also NeoGOS and NuSweet.
- Partner brands on its site: collagen (Naticol, Keragen-IV, Vollagen, KoAct, kollaGen II-xs), plant protein (RisaPro, Peasipro), botanicals (BacoMind, Turmacin, GutGard, LongJaX, Saffr'Activ, Liboost), VegD3, K2VITAL, Livaux, Actazin, PureMune and Cognilipid.
- Size: no filed accounts; "more than 60 team members worldwide" (March 2026); Owler estimates 25 to 100 million dollars revenue, ZoomInfo 6.9 million dollars. No funding rounds, investment, sale process or advisers found.
- Europe: no AIDP office found; it exhibited Magtein at Fi Europe 2025 and Vitafoods.

sessions.title: Clasado (Bimuno GOS): possible sale
sessions.to_check: The CEO's name (the dictated note reads "the CEO pair"; Per Rehné is Clasado's CEO on Companies House, to confirm); the currency of the sales and price figures; whether the price assumes the parent loan is written off.
sessions.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's note, 17 Nov 2026)
sessions.notes:
Nathan's note from day 1 of FiE, 17 Nov 2026, dictated, verbatim (the part about this company; his opening line first):

Quick note from the first day of FIE I've been speaking to lots of people about things and all of the big takeaways are three specific companies that either are out for sale or will be up for sale in the next 2 to 3 years.

The first is Clasado own bimuno GOS , their company doing about 3 million in sales, not at all profitable yet but hope to be in the next two years. The significant growth potential with that ingredient they could easily be doing 8 to 10 million. I know the CEO pair quite well and he told me that they would be looking for 10 to 12,000,000 probably as a sale price.

summary.Summary:
On the first day of FiE, Clasado's chief executive told Nathan the company would look for a sale price of probably 10 to 12 million. Nathan knows him well. Clasado sells about 3 million a year, is not yet profitable and hopes to be within two years. Nathan sees room for its one ingredient, Bimuno GOS, to reach 8 to 10 million in sales.

Clasado is a Reading company owned through Jersey by Liechtenstein trusts. Per Rehné has been chief executive since 2019, and the dictated "CEO pair" is most likely "CEO Per". It sells one ingredient, Bimuno, a prebiotic made from milk sugar, protected by patents and backed by more than 25 clinical trials, two of them in athletes. It has no authorised health claim in the EU but has claims in Australia, Colombia and other markets.

Its accounts show a loss every year. Turnover was £5.1 million in 2024, but that included the Bimuno consumer business, sold to ELEAT at the start of 2025, so the ingredient business alone fits the 3 million Nathan heard. The company owes its Jersey parent £41.8 million, and its auditors have twice flagged doubt over its ability to continue without that support. In October 2026 it appointed ACI Group as its UK and Ireland distributor.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Price talk from the chief executive: "they would be looking for 10 to 12,000,000 probably as a sale price" (notes).
- Size and profit as Nathan heard them: about 3 million in sales, "not at all profitable yet but hope to be in the next two years" (notes).
- Nathan's view of the upside: "they could easily be doing 8 to 10 million" (notes).
- The filed accounts show losses of £2.5 to £4.0 million a year from 2021 to 2024, a £41.8 million interest-free loan from the Jersey parent repayable on demand, and net liabilities of £38.6 million at the end of 2025. My reading: what happens to that loan decides what a buyer really pays.
- My reading: the business is now ingredient-only. The consumer Bimuno brand went to ELEAT on 1 Jan 2025, so the 2024 turnover of £5.1 million overstates today's ingredient sales.
- No authorised EU health claim: EFSA found no cause and effect for the gut-discomfort claim. Claims exist in Australia (29 relationships) and Colombia (11).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: the most concrete of the three FiE leads, with a price named by the chief executive, whom Nathan knows well (notes).
- My reading: a sale price of 10 to 12 million is about two to four times the sales Nathan heard, before the parent loan is settled.
- My reading: Bimuno fits our sports and healthy-ageing work. It has athlete trials from Nottingham Trent (2016 and 2026; the 2026 trial reported less gut-barrier damage at 2.75 g a day for six weeks, per Clasado's release) and trials in people aged 52 to 65.
- My reading: without an EU claim, selling it in Europe rests on the studies, not on a claim on pack.
- My reading: short of buying, Clasado is now a business-to-business supplier building distribution; ACI Group took the UK and Ireland in October 2026, so Vita Actives could look at other territories or be a competitor for that role.

summary.Research:
Desk research on public sources, 17 Nov 2026. Nothing Nathan was told went into a search.
- Identity: Clasado Limited, Companies House 05268862, incorporated 25 Oct 2004, Reading; from University of Reading research. US subsidiary Clasado, Inc. (Delaware).
- Ownership: wholly owned by Clasado Biosciences Limited (Jersey). Ultimate controlling party Lexus Trust (Vaduz, Liechtenstein), "financed by Plexus Trust". Four people with significant control, each controlling a trust's trustees, resident in Liechtenstein or Switzerland; two more ceased on 6 May 2026. Ownership before December 2018 was not found; no funding rounds are recorded.
- Chief executive: Per Rehné, formerly commercial director of OptiBiotix; director from 4 Mar 2019, reported as CEO on 13 Mar 2019. Graham Waters was CEO in 2016.
- Product: Bimuno GOS, made from lactose with enzymes from *B. bifidum* NCIMB 41171, as powder or syrup; patents US 7883874 and CA 2520043. The company states GRAS status, EU and UK novel foods compliance, Halal and Kosher, and "100+ claims available for select markets". More than 130 publications and 25+ clinical trials (company figures).
- Accounts (Clasado Limited, audited): turnover £3,108,014 and loss £2,511,144 (2021); £2,616,421 and £2,833,954 (2022); £3,322,615 and £3,969,771 (2023); £5,130,284 and £2,565,605 (2024). 2024 gross profit £3,183,553. 2025 filed as small-company accounts with no profit and loss account: net liabilities £38,572,000, parent loan £41,766,000, 23 staff. Going-concern material uncertainty flagged in the 2022 and 2024 accounts.
- Consumer business: sold on 1 Jan 2025 to H2Nutrition Ltd, announced in April 2025 as a sale to ELEAT (products, customers and a UK licence). Inference: H2Nutrition is ELEAT's company, as ELEAT's co-founder is its director.
- Manufacturing: no plant named; plant at cost totals £200,660, fully depreciated. Inference: production is outsourced.
- Distribution: ACI Group, UK and Ireland (21 Oct 2026); Pharmanutra, Italy; Prokopton, France; Globofarm, India; Phytonet, 14 markets. Bimuno Pet launched October 2024.
- Changes: auditor changed November 2024; the sister research company was folded in and dissolved on 22 Sep 2026; new VP Sales (October 2025) and Asia-Pacific director (April 2026). No public sale process or advisers.
- Competitors: FrieslandCampina GOS (16 Australian claim relationships). Inference: Ingredion, Yakult/Nissin GOS, and inulin and FOS suppliers (Beneo, Sensus).
- Sources:

  - [Nutrition Insight, "Eleat acquires Clasado's Bimuno supplement portfolio", 7 Apr 2025](https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/clasado-eleat-bimuno-acquisition-prebiotic-gut-health-supplements.html)
  - [EFSA Journal opinion 3756, Bimuno GOS and GI discomfort](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/pl/efsajournal/pub/3756)

sessions.notes:
Nathan's note from day 1 of FiE, 17 Nov 2026, dictated, verbatim (the part about this company; his opening line first):

Quick note from the first day of FIE I've been speaking to lots of people about things and all of the big takeaways are three specific companies that either are out for sale or will be up for sale in the next 2 to 3 years.

Finally there is a company called Fairfield Nutech, who offend I know called Jordan runs. He told me they were looking at a 2 to 3 year exit plan. Their specialist protein House with interesting tech technologies.

summary.Summary:
On the first day of FiE, Jordan, a friend of Nathan's who runs a company dictated as "Fairfield Nutech", told him they are looking at a two to three year exit plan. Nathan describes it as a specialist protein house with interesting technologies.

The company is most likely Fayrefield Nutratek, a sports-protein business in Crewe set up in June 2025. Its director Jordan Donohue has owned 20% from the start, and the name, the first name and the protein technology all match, though nothing public calls him chief executive. The rest is owned by Fayrefield's UK dairy-trading group and its Danish sister company, 37.5% each, with 5% held by a second director.

Nutratek sells whey, milk-protein and casein ingredients, including clear whey and hydrolysates, application systems for drinks, yoghurt, powders and bars, and a protein coffee. Since May 2026 it has been the exclusive UK and Western Europe distributor of Jenerise creatine, which competes with CreaWin.

It has filed no accounts yet. The UK parent group turned over £254.8 million in 2024. A Danish private equity firm took 60% of the Danish parent in late 2025, so any sale needs both parents to agree. No public sign of a sale was found.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Jordan told Nathan "they were looking at a 2 to 3 year exit plan" (notes).
- Nathan's description: a "specialist protein House with interesting tech technologies" (notes).
- My reading: the company is most likely Fayrefield Nutratek Ltd (Companies House 16494089), whose director and 20% founding shareholder is Jordan Patrick Donohue; nothing public names him chief executive.
- Ownership at founding: The Fayrefield Group Ltd 37.5%, Fayrefield Ingredients Holdings A/S (Denmark) 37.5%, Jordan Donohue 20%, George Hopkins 5%. A sister company, Fayrefield Proteins Ltd, was set up on 17 Jul 2026 with the UK group at 75%, Donohue 20% and Hopkins 5%.
- My reading: an exit for Jordan may mean his 20% stake rather than a sale of the whole company, since the two Fayrefield parents hold 75%.
- Nutratek is the exclusive UK and Western Europe distributor of Jenerise Cr.01 creatine (May 2026), a direct competitor to CreaWin.
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: one of three companies Nathan named at FiE as for sale or soon to be (notes); he lists it as a possible acquisition and partner.
- My reading: as a competitor today, Jenerise creatine meets CreaWin in our territory, and Nutratek's clear whey and drink systems sit beside IsoClr: Pea.
- My reading: as a partner, its application know-how in drinks, bars and yoghurt could carry our ingredients into finished formats; a dairy-protein house may want a plant protein such as IsoClr: Pea beside its whey.
- My reading: as an acquisition, the value is in people and the group's dairy supply rather than owned patents or plant, and the company is under 18 months old with no accounts.
- Context from SANS: Alan Johnstone argued that whey stays expensive because cheese output grows about 1.5% a year while demand grows 10% or more (unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of). A whey business depends on that supply, which Fayrefield's dairy group provides.

summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm with Nathan that "Fairfield Nutech" is Fayrefield Nutratek and Jordan is Jordan Donohue.
- Ask Jordan whether the exit plan is for the whole company or his stake, and whether both Fayrefield parents back it.
- Ask whether the Jenerise creatine exclusivity would pass to a buyer.
- Look at a partnership short of buying: Nutratek's drink and bar systems with IsoClr: Pea.

sessions.title: The Challenge and Opportunity of Our Ageing Population

speakers.name: David Weinkove
speakers.organisation: British Society for Research on Ageing (BSRA); Durham University
speakers.role: Emeritus Chair, British Society for Research on Ageing; Professor, Durham University

sessions.to_check: Whether Nathan attended. No recording; slides only. The second person pictured on the call-to-action slide (slide 9) is not named.
sessions.added_by: Claude (from the printed agenda, Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
David Weinkove, Professor at Durham University and Emeritus Chair of the British Society for Research on Ageing (BSRA), gave the first talk on the day's agenda. His subject was why slowing ageing matters, and why it is hard to prove.

He opened with a strong claim: our ageing population is a bigger threat than climate change, through the cost of living, pressure on health services and tension in society. A population pyramid of the UK in 2026 set the scene.

He then set prevention against treatment and argued that ageing is malleable. In England, people in the least deprived areas live 70.7 years in good health; in the most deprived, 51.9.

The science has three fundamentals. Ageing speeds up with time, people grow more different from each other, and the body holds its balance less well. That makes trials hard: they need large numbers of healthy but ageing people over several years, and funding and approval are difficult.

His call to action had three parts. Make the case that keeping people healthy for longer is good for everyone. Make trials long enough to measure ageing. Bring industry, charities, government and universities together. The BSRA, with over 300 members from academia and industry, asked the room to talk to it.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The frame: "Our ageing population is a bigger threat than climate change", because of the cost of living, pressure on health services and societal tensions (slide 2).
- Ageing is malleable: in England (ONS, 2018 to 2020, in the Chief Medical Officer's Annual Report 2023), the least deprived 10% of small areas live 70.7 years in good health and 15.6 in poorer health; the most deprived 51.9 and 26.4 (slide 5).
- Three fundamentals of ageing: the rate of ageing accelerates with time, variation between individuals increases, and homeostasis declines (slide 6).
- Trials to slow ageing need large numbers and several years, ideally in people who are healthy but ageing, and funding and approval are challenging (slide 7).
- The call to action: make the case for healthy longevity, make trials long enough to measure ageing, and have industry, charities, government and universities work together (slide 9).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance low: no ingredient or product is named. The talk sets the public-health and research frame for healthy ageing, not a market (slide 2) (slide 9).
- My reading: years in good health, not lifespan, is the frame our healthy-ageing pitches for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea already use. The healthy-life-expectancy gap is a public figure (ONS, Chief Medical Officer) a brand deck could cite (slide 5).
- His point on trials (slide 7). My reading: "slowing ageing" stays out of reach as a supplement claim for years; muscle, strength and function endpoints remain the practical route for creatine and protein.
- The BSRA invites industry to talk to it and counts industry among its members (slide 8) (slide 9). My reading: a route to academic partners if we ever fund a long healthy-ageing study.
- Context from the next talk: Nick Stene of Euromonitor said 2026 is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment, and that demographics explain about 30 to 40% of consumer-health growth through people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). Weinkove's slides frame the ageing population itself as the challenge; the two views differ in emphasis.
summary.Quotes:
- "Our ageing population is a bigger threat than climate change" (slide 2)
- "Make the case: keeping people healthy for longer is good for everyone" (slide 9)
- "Make trials long enough to measure ageing" (slide 9)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask the BSRA how industry members join and whether it brokers long-term healthy-ageing trials with industry partners.
- Find the Chief Medical Officer's Annual Report 2023 (Health in an Ageing Society) for the healthy-life-expectancy figures, if a brand deck needs them.
- Confirm whether Nathan attended.

sessions.transcript:
# Euromonitor: who is winning in the healthspan economy: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Nick Stene - Euromonitor - Healthspan Summit", https://otter.ai/u/I6bgV_HNiWcf94HGErPRO0tu7Hs, recorded 10 Nov 2026 09:24, 23m 32s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Stephen Daniells (NutraIngredients): Okay, so our first speaker is going to set the scene for us. Nick Steen is senior global insight manager for consumer health for Euro Monitor, and he's going to tell us who is winning in the health fan economy. Thank you. Thank you.
[00:20] Speaker 1 (Nick Stene): Good morning. Right. So my name's Nick. I'll get into who I am in a minute. I've got 20 minutes, and in that time, I wish to impart three things. One, where is the money going? Second thing, who's getting paid, and what messages are actually winning premium. So I'll show you some growth numbers, and I'll show you which prices are actually achieved in the market around particular claims and ingredients. And lastly, I want to just emphasize the proof topic. It is probably the most important thing strategically going on within the BBS space right now, and I'll get around to explaining why. If I look at background, so I've got 30 years doing business decision making, 20 brand side, then 10 in research consulting, and I'm a psychologist. I mention that just because you'll notice it creeps in every now and again into how I think and how I talk about these things. First of all, some context. So if we look at the total industry, we've got as I scope it, we've got a total value of 373 billion vitamins and dietary supplements as one of the big growth areas. If we look at it within the pie chart for size, you can see how it breaks out. OTC treatments, sports nutrition, and weight management and well-being. It's currently about 5% growth. If you take out inflation, it's 1.5. That's down half a point into further stagnation overall if we rip out prices. So this is this is not a fast demand growth environment where some parts of it are actually growing faster than others. If we look particularly at that treatment area, rip out inflation, and that's actually gone negative this year, and that's created one of the first big things I want to just mention, which is this is the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment. That's quite a big milestone in terms of changes to the market. And if you look at the difference between VDS and OTC, that gap is only going to get bigger. Then let's look at that in future terms. So this is looking at the cash added between now and 2031 from all the forecast data that we pick up from our partners. And if we look at the immediate growth year on year, that's 2027 versus this year. If we look long term, this is an average K gap out to 2031, and the bubble size is the cash. It's the size of the prize that will be added between now and 2031. And one of the things that jumps out is yes, there's some bubbles which are more attractive than others, but then let's add a cost element to this. So OTC has been hit by the tariffs more than the rest of the health industry. If we then think about what's going on in the Middle East, the dependence on the active pharmaceutical ingredients coming out of India, coming out of China, are creating a greater liability. So the cost of that, the disruption of that has been greater for treatment than it has for VDS, and the future one is around the European wastewater. Again, that's intended to hit the OTC space more than it is going to hit the prevention space in VDS. So that that's a nice big block of value for OTC, but it's got quite serious profit questions around it in terms of the business model and going forward. Then let's look at the protein one around sports protein products. This is then getting hit by the problems with premium weight, and I've got data showing the shelf a 20% plus pass through in physical pricing, but that's 30 to 40% overall. If you then take into account shrinkage in packaging and all the other techniques that the brands are trying to do to actually absorb this cost. So the protein one probably starts to get solved in supply because it's scarcity driven around premium way around 2027 back end, 2028 earliest, and that's starting to get solved. There's years of trauma left inside of that one, so that block also has questions in terms of future profit. So that makes the block for dietary supplements even more attractive. This is revenue, but if we think in profit terms, that's actually the most attractive by a long way for a lot of what's going on, and that is then leading to a migration of money heading towards dietary supplements, particularly premium dietary supplements. Both we can see it within line extensions, we can see it inside with brand actions at the tactical level, but at the strategic level, we also see it driving mergers and acquisition strategy. And there's quite a lot of finance. I see about eight to $9 billion in motion right now around fighting over positioning. Some of that's coming from outside of health and venture capital and private equity getting involved inside of this to fight over that space. So it's just to let you know that that area is competitive and it's going to become more competitive over time. Then we come to the first speed bump when we're into any topic about health span. What do we actually mean by the term? And I reckon if we got 10 of us up on the stage and asked 10 people what health span is, we would collectively come to 10 different answers. Some will include aspects of it. Some will exclude. It will be an interesting conversation. So, if I think about how I am looking at health span and measuring health span, I'm starting to perceive this as a funnel, and this is coming from the research into how consumers are shopping and how they do message recognition and what they're actually looking for. So, I think at the edge of this funnel, the cutting edge of this area, we've got naming on the product itself. This is the actual SKU name, and it's directly into age. It's directly into life stage. It's directly into the core messaging for what we're here in this room to talk about. And one of the things to point out is mitochondrial is one of the elements that's appearing inside of here. I'll come back to that in a minute. Then we end up with a broader health span messaging that can appear anywhere on the pack. It doesn't necessarily mean that the skew is all about health span. It's touching into the space, and then we've got the protection messages, and this takes us to a much bigger part of the funnel, and this is immune system. It's antioxidant. It's a much broader message structure. We've got to separate them and think of them differently because they've got very different commercial profiles in terms of how well they're doing and who's winning and where that's winning. If I think about that funnel, then across different areas, and I'm going down to 18 markets now because these are the ones with the cleanest data to be able to do the analysis as to what fits and where. So if I look at total value from the supplements, this is from our total market size, and we look at that edge. It's niche, but it's growing. I'll come to growth rates in a second, and yes, you can think it's quite low within Asia, but look at the cash value difference between Asia and Europe, top six. This is where it's playing out in terms of scale. If we then think about the broader health plan messaging, it kicks in at this larger level, and when we get into the protection messaging, we're talking about half the shelf, pretty much. So, in terms of scale, that one aspect of this, but also I did analysis in terms of what's achieving a premium versus the rest of the shelf, and the edge is the part that's actually exceeding the rest of it. The actual broader health span messaging is appearing on cheap product as much as it's appearing on expensive product. There's a degree to which the message is getting diluted as part of the step-up structure at this moment. So the the second thing I really want to get across is we've got to name the need, and the more we name the need, the more we get the benefits out of this space, both on the growth side, but also on the getting paid for it side of it with premium achievement. If we look at growth rates, this is online growth. I'll just state that outright. So the VBS number is probably larger than you're expecting. One of the things to point out is the edge is where we're seeing the exceptional growth, and we do see actual growth within the broader messaging. It's more successful within the shops because of the trust angle than it is online. There's a degree of trust leaking into the online situation around who can you trust, what messages can you trust. People are making incredibly strong promises without a lot of background as to why they make it and the evidence behind it. You could obviously think that it's all about the demographics, but when I tried to correlate and look at all of the things that drive a market that's got a rising health span number within the nutrition side of it, I got some surprises. So it's not really correlating around the existing size of the aging population. That doesn't count, and it's not particularly around the spend on health right now. That didn't really match against where this is growing particularly quickly. I also did a check because when we looked at this in 2022 and 2023, we saw that the COVID scare had led to a large amount of investment heading in this direction that has stopped having any kind of relationship to which markets this is growing in. One of the other things that I did find is actually spend on self-cow and OTC spend that is actually on the border of being statistically significant around a relationship to which markets this is growing in, and there's a logic to that around when we have conditions and we start to spend on condition support. That's the place where effectively the nutritional angle for health plans is going to resonate the most. We've got e-commerce as arising. This is access based, but I didn't see a difference between total shelf VDS and the health plan product. So this is just about access generally, and we get into one of the other aspects where it's it is about the aging population, but it's about how many people enter a new life stage in a given year, and that is actually driving some of this is not to do with the base population right now. It's to do with people arriving at a transitional moment, and I can explain insight. Income was part of it, but it was not that strong apart. I can explain within consumer poll demographics about 30 to 40% of the shift in the growth period. If I look at what else is going on, I think the push side of it and the creation of demand from the brand messaging is explaining about another third or so of the actual growth that we're seeing. And then, when I go into this, I can find anecdotal evidence on the survey side that the relationship between employer and employee is driving another aspect of this. If we think about the price of being ill, it's not just about the symptoms. It's not just about the issues. It's about the time off work, and we are seeing quite a substantial shift in the relationship between employer and employee, and the penalties potentially across the world on being out of work are right, and that is affecting the whole dynamic around why prevention is winning over treatment, and it's actually most manifest within the health span area. So there's an economic aspect to this. It's an investment more than it is actually just something ephemeral and something emotional. There are there are fiscal aspects to this. There are rational aspects to this around protecting income. If we look at what is actually growing, this is growing at the shelf rather than sales growth, just to be clear. So along the x-axis, you see that the rate of new products and messaging arriving at the shelf, and then on the y-axis you can see the premium level that's being achieved. And we can see longevity and healthy aging in the U.S. is the element that's growing fastest and getting paid very strongly followed. I am seeing menopause generally actually losing its premium. It's becoming ubiquitous inside of the messaging, but within it, we do have this new 40 plus element targeting around perimenopause, and that is still achieving a premium. It's not as fast in growth terms. It's not as big a message, but it's coming and it's coming fast. If I then think broader, the menopause and the prostate messaging, prostate aid that men, I'll come to the different life stage messaging in a minute. That started to slow down a little bit, and it's lost the premium. It's back into how many launches are being positioned from value brands and from private label. If we think about the beauty angle to it, so skin is ubiquitous. It's one of the biggest messages inside of this space. It peaked in 2025, and it's actually starting to slow down the new launches and what's coming to market? It's still one of the stronger areas, but behind it, and my my beauty colleagues have warned me, the next big one is hair, and I can see it already within the hair loss treatment space. It's one of the fastest growth categories this year, but I can also see it appearing inside the nutrition element of it, and hair is achieving a premium, and it's actually appearing in weights over the shelf. If we look at the immune system, I'm going to come to magnesium in a second and talk about what's going on with magnesium. But the immune system has also peaked, and it's sitting there. It's just trucking away. It's one of the workhorses of this market in terms of maintaining value and cash scale. If we then go across the pond and we look at Europe, it's roughly the same pattern. One thing jumped out at me, which is slightly different: the messaging around mitochondrial is a lot stronger in Europe already than it is in the U.S. at this stage, and some of this is to do with regulatory framework and what messaging is allowed inside of one process in Nathan. Health span messaging, in and of itself, healthy aging messaging in Europe is a tougher sell, and some of it isn't making it to the physical shelf. Some of it's only occurring online. So different wording, but the same sort of pattern in terms of what's going on. If I think about that magnesium angle, I'm into the issues around ingredients and the lifespan of ingredients commanding a premium. We've got a number of the magnesium variants that are tied to specific need, and what's fascinating in terms of their pattern, they've arrived at the shelf in far greater number, but they've lost their premium in the act of doing so, and they've turned into footballs, and they're being kicked around on price right now, which is, if you look at it, ironic that those are actually achieving less of a premium overall than some of the more basic forms. L3 and eight is escaping this so far. It's attached to the cognitive side of it. It's doing well around launches and into premium achievement. But look at the pattern. If it ends up as another football, it's not going to be long before it actually starts to bleed and lose its premium. So the pattern I can see is we get proof of benefit, we get to premium achievement, we reach popularity, and the scale goes, the awareness rises, and then we're entitled. And this battle has played out a few times within Magnesium so far. And so one of the things is a bit melodramatic as a statement, but popularity is the death knell on premium. It's more complicated than that, but you get the idea. I've also seen it at the cutting edge. So NAD Plus has been the breakout. It escaped niche last year, and we see it growing three times larger on the shelf in the U.S. inside of an 18-month period. So enormous levels of change, and what I see is a recovery-ish in 2026, with greater use of stacks. So NAD plus with spermidine, NAD plus with resveratrol, and a number of other combinations. So we've got back some of the premium as new launches have hit the market. But you can see the general trend with Europe not not far behind in terms of the pattern. I think we're into popularity and we're near to price war. It's still got a premium, but it's lost quite a substantial amount of that premium. And that brings us into one of the structures around trust and proof. If ingredients lose premium over time, what's next? And NAD Plus has been and will continue to be a really strong workhorse in this space. It's got lots of value adds in terms of messaging and what we can do with it in product terms. But what's sitting behind? From what I can see, there's a number of ingredients that might be the next thing. But postbiotics is at this moment in time kicking ass, and if I look at the growth rate, if I look at the messaging it's getting into, it's got really strong connections into GLP-1, and it's achieving one of the strongest premiums at this moment in time. So if I want to point in any one direction, that's the one that's got my attention, and I'm studying that one quite a lot. So what's next? We need a pipeline of premiums. You can't just rely on something to be there and shine forever. If we get into the life stages, so I can see menopause is starting to slow down, but within it, the perimenopause messaging is rising fast. It's on one minute at this point, and that's doubled in a year. Underlying that is the number of ingredients that are driving it. If I look at the male equivalent andropause, blokes do not seem to be buying to a life stretch, so they don't really want the label, and they certainly don't want to walk into a part of the store that's labeled up as Andrew Police Paul. What they do want to talk about is testosterone and performance. I made the mistake of going to one of those sites and dwelling for a couple of minutes, and I'm now being hunted across all of my profiles online with how do I feel like a man and would I like her? How could it's everywhere. I mean, I cannot now go and watch a cat video, which is what the internet was actually designed for. If I look at the the direction, men get a performance message; they also get an organ, and it might not be the one that everyone was expecting. But effectively, the prostate is a sufficient source of fear that it's driving a certain amount of traffic, a certain amount of effort here. I have eight. I talk about them a bit too much. One of the reasons I talk about them so often is because this is one of the most interesting and exciting growth profiles that I have seen in 30 years. So it broke 100 million inside of year one, it's currently on target to hit around 220 to 230 in year two. They are projecting 400 million in year three, and they just picked up. Let's just skip through all the junk. They picked up a billion in investment funding earlier on this year, and it's because of. There we go. They have a subscription model with an acquisition rate that's allowing them to get to a profit level from investment, which is pain all over the market. So that's attracted the investment, and that's why they're going so bullish in terms of their growth. If if you want to study two brands that are absolutely nailing proof, I am eight is one of them. I would also draw your attention to ancient and brave. It is one of the most incredible structures in terms of how how trusted they have made themselves within their loyal shopper base in such a hot tithing. So one of the other things I'm observing is if you are solving a problem, either you'll fix it or you won't. But either one of those leads to you no longer being needed. If instead you're about trying to facilitate someone's perfect life, you're not asking them to admit they're imperfect, which is one of the first things that consumers are struggling with right now. So I think, honestly, what I'm starting to see is this difference in messaging and positioning. It's the same thing. It's collagen, but it's multiple ways of actually communicating collagen, which answer completely different needs in the emotional range. And one of those has got a long-term survival within the human basket. The other one is either going to die because it solved the problem. There's no more problem, or it's failed to fix the problem. So why would I continue taking it? So I've got four takeaways. One, see it with proof. That's the part that's paying. That's the part that's growing. The more specific we get, the more evidence we've got around it, the better. Also, we've got to know the ingredient life stage that we're operating with, and what's the pipeline? What's next? What's coming? We've got to segment and price this. I think we are failing as a species, all women, and we're failing particularly the age band heading into perimenopause. This is from personal experience on the journey with my wife as well. It is an absolute horror show. So I think there's a lot that can be done. Just she didn't get listened to and she didn't get referred to a specialist until I was in the room, and I'm just confused. We we are not doing very well inside of this area. There's a lot more that we can do. It's nice to see that the 40 plus messaging and perimenopause is finally finding voice, but there's a lot more to go inside of this space. And we've got design proof for the three gatekeepers. The shopper is only one lens. We know that the healthcare professionals are one of the advice structures we've got to appeal to. We've got to educate, and we've got to win them. But keep in mind, around the corner comes the agentic commerce side of it, and the agent looks at proof through a completely different lens to a human being. And we've got to look after with all of those assets, those images, those materials, they've got to serve multiple missions. So that's my last point for today. Thank you very much. If you want to
[23:16] Stephen Daniells (NutraIngredients): thank you, Nick. In the interest of time, we're going to move on really quickly. But as Nick said, he is around, so hunt him down, ask your questions. Thank you so much, Nick. All right, we're going to keep going, and next we're going to introduce Emma Hudson, who is senior insights director.

summary.Summary:
Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager for consumer health at Euromonitor International, opened the Healthspan Summit. His question was where the money in healthspan is going and which messages earn a premium.

He started with the market. Consumer health grows about 5%, only 1.5% without inflation, and this is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment. Medicines sold over the counter and sports protein are both under profit pressure, so money, including billions in deal finance, is moving to premium dietary supplements.

Within healthspan, products that name a specific need or life stage earn a premium, while broad wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike. Ingredients follow a life cycle: proof brings a premium, popularity brings scale, then a price war. Magnesium forms have gone that way and NAD+ is close, with postbiotics leading what queues behind it. IM8, one product meant to replace a shelf of supplements, was his example of a brand winning on proof and trust.

His conclusion: lead with proof, know where each ingredient is in its life cycle, segment and price for specific groups such as women entering perimenopause, and design proof for shoppers, healthcare professionals and the AI agents that will increasingly shop for them.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).
- Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].
- Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].
- Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).
- NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
- IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- He expects premium whey supply to start being solved around the back end of 2027, 2028 at the earliest, and sees sports protein brands passing on 20% or more on shelf, 30 to 40% with smaller packs [00:20]. Alan Johnstone at SANS Europe expects whey to stay structurally expensive, with announced capacity running to 2028 (unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of). My reading: both views point to protein margins staying tight through 2027, which keeps blends and alternatives such as IsoClr: Pea on brands' agendas.
- His ingredient life cycle applies to creatine: proof brings a premium and popularity erodes it [00:20] (photo 3). My reading: CreaWin's case to brands should rest on its own evidence and a clear benefit, not on creatine's popularity.
- Healthy-ageing customers pay for named needs and proof, and in Europe mitochondrial wording is already established [00:20]. My reading: our healthy-ageing pitches should name the need and the evidence.
- AI shopping agents read proof differently [00:20]. My reading: our evidence files should be structured and machine-readable.
- Relevance high: healthy-ageing market structure and sports protein economics.

- The speaker was introduced as Nick Steen; the title slide gives Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager, Consumer Health, Euromonitor International [00:00] (photo 1).
- Market: he gave consumer health as "373 billion", growing about 5%, or 1.5 without inflation, half a point down; treatment has gone negative in real terms [00:20]. The slide gives USD 373 billion, +5% in current terms (3.5% price rises) and +1.5% without inflation ("demand stagnation") (photo 2).
- Growth by category, 2025 then 2026: vitamins and dietary supplements 5.9% and 5.6%; OTC 3.4% and 3.2%; sports nutrition 13.3% and 12.5%; weight management and wellbeing 0.2% and 0.3%. The slide's line: "2026 is the year when we started spending more on prevention than we do on treatment" (photo 2).
- OTC is hit hardest by tariffs, by dependence on active pharmaceutical ingredients from India and China, and, next, by European wastewater rules [00:20].
- Sports protein, as he said it: he has shelf data showing a 20% plus pass-through in physical pricing, 30 to 40% overall once pack shrinkage and other absorption moves are counted. On premium whey supply: "So the protein one probably starts to get solved in supply because it's scarcity driven around premium way around 2027 back end, 2028 earliest", with "years of trauma" left [00:20].
- Growth is stronger in shops than online, where trust is leaking; demographics explain about 30 to 40% of growth (people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population), brand push about another third, and employers' attitudes to time off work more [00:20].
- On the US shelf, longevity and healthy ageing grow fastest and earn a strong premium; menopause is losing its premium while 40-plus and perimenopause still earn one; prostate has lost its premium; skin peaked in 2025 and hair is next; immune has peaked but remains a workhorse [00:20].
- Europe follows the same pattern, but mitochondrial messaging is already stronger than in the US, partly because of what the regulatory framework allows, and healthy-ageing messaging is "a tougher sell", some of it only online [00:20].
- Magnesium forms in Europe, January to August 2026 against 2025, read approximately from the chart (price index against matched peers, change in share of products): carbonate about 1.4 and 0%; oxide about 0.75 and 3%; citrate about 0.95 and 13%; bisglycinate about 0.65 and 42%; taurate about 0.55 and 43%; malate about 0.55 and 48%; L-threonate (cognitive) about 1.17 and 49%. The slide's line: "Popularity is a consistent death [k]nell for premium [achieve]ment." (photo 3). Otter heard L-threonate as "L3 and eight" [00:20].
- NAD+ escaped niche last year and grew three times on the US shelf in 18 months; stacks with spermidine and resveratrol won back some premium in 2026, but it is near price war [00:20]. The slide's NAD+ family price index (NAD+, NADH, NR, NMN, NMNH): US 1.84 in 2024, 1.28 in 2025, 1.43 in 2026 to date; Europe 1.68, 1.50 and 1.32 (photo 4).
- Queuing behind NAD+, US 2026 (share growth, price index): postbiotics +48%, 2.83; urolithin A +17%, 1.37; TMG +19%, 1.23; fisetin +22%, 1.14; spermidine +45%, 1.13. The slide's line: "What's next? Because nothing stays shiny and new forev[er]" (photo 4).
- Postbiotics are growing fast, have "really strong connections into GLP-1" and earn one of the strongest premiums; he is watching them most closely. In his words: "But postbiotics is at this moment in time kicking ass" [00:20].
- Life stage, US products per 10,000 supplement products, 2024, 2025 and 2026 to date: testosterone 171, 182, 163; prostate 70, 85, 98; menopause 46, 64, 73; andropause 0, 1, 2. The slides: perimenopause is picking up fast while menopause slows; andropause is "near non-existent on the shelf"; testosterone is more than twice the size of menopause on the shelf, stalled in the US, still rising in Europe and getting cheaper, with fading spikes in tongkat ali, tribulus and shilajit; prostate support now rises fast (photo 5) (photo 6).
- Men do not buy into an andropause label; they respond to testosterone, performance and prostate messages [00:20] (photo 6).
- IM8, as he said it: over 100 million in year one, on target for 220 to 230 in year two, 400 million projected for year three, and a billion raised on a profitable subscription model [00:20]. The slide: year-two revenue guidance USD 220 to 230 million and 2027 full-year guidance over USD 400 million; US online sales peaked in Q4 2025 and eased slightly in Q1 and Q2 2026; the US is by far its largest market, ahead of the UK and Canada (photo 7).
- Why IM8 wins, from the slide: one product replaces a shelf (90 ingredients, positioned to replace 16 other supplements); celebrity equity and a science council, driving word of mouth; subscription economics a lender can fund, with USD 1.44 of declared gross profit per USD 1 of acquisition; and an AI-native acquisition engine across 43 markets. "IM8 nailed "trust" in all its flavours" (photo 7).
- He named IM8 and Ancient + Brave as brands nailing proof [00:20]. Nathan's note: IM8 "is winning a lot in the market, alongside Ancient+Brave" (notes).
- Positioning that facilitates "someone's perfect life" lasts longer than solving a problem, which ends when it is fixed or fails; collagen can be sold either way [00:20]. The slide sets "something wrong [with] you our product can fix" (joints, wrinkles, ageing, collagen deficiency) against "Aspire to a life free of imperfection" (vitality, performance, radiance, wellbeing): "you never stop taking something that is part of who you want to be" (photo 8).
- His takeaways: lead with proof; know the ingredient's life stage and the pipeline behind it; segment and price, with women heading into perimenopause badly served; and design proof for three gatekeepers: shoppers, healthcare professionals and agentic commerce [00:20].

files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Nick presents an analysis of the healthspan economy, highlighting a strategic shift from disease treatment to preventive dietary supplements.

## Market Dynamics
**Nick** outlines a significant transition in the consumer health industry, noting that for the first time, spending on prevention has surpassed spending on treatment. While the total vitamins and dietary supplements (VDS) market is valued at $373 billion, growth is uneven. 
*   **OTC** treatments face challenges including tariffs, supply chain dependencies on India and China, and environmental regulations regarding wastewater.
*   **Sports nutrition** faces profit pressures due to high protein costs and packaging shrinkage.
*   **Dietary supplements** are identified as the most attractive segment for investment and mergers/acquisitions, with $8 to $9 billion currently in motion via venture capital and private equity.

## Growth Drivers
**Nick** identifies several key areas driving premium pricing and market expansion:
*   **Healthspan Messaging:** Consumers are moving toward specific "edge" messaging such as mitochondrial health, rather than broad protection messages like immunity. 
*   **Life Stages:** There is rapid growth in perimenopause targeting (40+ demographic), whereas general menopause messaging is losing its premium. For men, the focus shifts from "andropause" labels to testosterone and performance.
*   **Ingredient Trends:** **NAD Plus** has seen massive growth in the U.S., though it is entering a phase where price wars may occur. **Postbiotics** are currently performing strongly with high premiums due to connections with **GLP-1**.
*   **Beauty & Hair:** While skin messaging is peaking, hair loss treatment is emerging as a fast-growing category that commands a premium.

## Strategic Takeaways
To maintain profitability, **Nick** suggests brands must move beyond simple problem-solving to facilitating a "perfect life" through emotional positioning. He emphasizes three critical pillars for success:
*   **Proof:** Brands must provide specific evidence and clinical backing to justify premium prices.
*   **Segmentation:** Companies must identify which life stage or specific ingredient cycle they are entering to avoid the "popularity death knell" where mass adoption erodes margins.
*   **Gatekeepers:** Success requires winning over three distinct groups: the shopper, healthcare professionals, and the emerging "agentic commerce" AI agents.

How can brands effectively design proof that satisfies both human healthcare professionals and automated AI shopping agents?

Action items (Otter's): none.

summary.Summary:
Ewa Hudson, Strategy & Insight Director at ReThink Global, Lumina Intelligence, presented a July 2026 survey of 10,500 consumers in nine countries. Her question: consumers are rewriting the rules of ageing, so is the industry ready to rewrite its own?

Her first point was that the longevity consumer is no longer old. Retired people mostly began thinking seriously about ageing in their 60s; people in full-time work mostly in their 30s. Younger people blame their genes less and put more faith in supplements, and one in four is actively pursuing anti-ageing.

Ageing well, she said, means having the vitality to keep reinventing yourself. Energy, stamina and physical strength is a top-three concern in every age band, and mobility, joint and bone health comes first for women from their mid-thirties. Needs shift with life stage and country, and GLP-1 treatment is moving UK users towards healthier habits.

Trust is the gap: in the UK, not enough proof was the most common hesitation about longevity supplements. Brands such as Niagen, Life Extension and Novos are moving from selling supplements to measuring and managing biological ageing. Her conclusion: applied and communicated science will be the number one trust creator, and the healthspan leaders of the next decade may be platforms that measure, manage and optimise ageing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Concern about ageing starts younger: retired respondents mostly began thinking seriously about it in their 60s (36%); in the deck's version of the chart, people working full-time mostly began in their 30s (about 30%, read from the chart). She called it "a generational shift" [00:04] (photo 1) (slide 4).
- The younger the respondent, the less they credit genetics and the more they credit supplements: genetics from 39% at 65 plus down to 21% at 18 to 24; supplements from 20% at 25 to 34 down to 12% at 65 plus [00:04] (slide 2) (slide 3).
- One in four is actively pursuing anti-ageing: 16% want to prevent premature ageing and 11% to reverse it, beside 52% who want to age slowly and healthily [00:04] (photo 2) (slide 5).
- Energy, stamina and strength is in the top three concerns of every age band, for men and women; mobility, joint and bone health is in the top three of every band from 35 to 44 up for both, and from 25 to 34 for women (photo 3) (slide 8).
- Trust is the gap. Biggest hesitation about longevity supplements in the UK: not enough proof 22%, cost 21%, don't believe claims 20%, safety concerns 20%. Across the survey, 36% already take supplements to counteract natural ageing [00:04] (slide 17) (slide 18).
- Brands are moving from product to platform: Niagen added telehealth, IV and injections, skincare and a drug pipeline; Life Extension sells ageing blood tests to take before and after supplements; Novos sells an at-home biological-age kit [00:04] (photo 4) (slide 9) (slide 19).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Energy, stamina and strength is a top-three ageing concern in every age band for both men and women (photo 3), and her list of what products must show starts with "Energy and physical strength" and ends with "Everyday activity and recovery" (slide 8). My reading: this is the concern our sports and active nutrition ingredients (CreaWin, IsoClr: Pea, Oxystorm) sit closest to, so healthy-ageing brands are a natural audience for them, pitched within what each ingredient's own evidence supports. The concerns slide gives an order, not percentages.
- People working full-time mostly start thinking about ageing in their 30s [00:04] (slide 4). My reading: the healthy-ageing buyer and the active adult our customers already sell to are increasingly the same person, which widens where sports ingredients can be pitched.
- 20% name amino acids and proteins among the categories most helpful for extending healthspan, behind vitamins (50%), omega-3 (39%), minerals (25%) and probiotics (22%) (slide 17). Muscle appears in her life-stage messages (UK women in their late 40s, US men in their late 30s), but 5% or fewer choose muscle mass or strength as their single most important goal (slide 10) (slide 11) (slide 13) (slide 14). My reading: muscle is a supporting healthy-ageing message, not the lead; energy, strength and everyday activity are the better door for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea.
- Not enough proof is the top UK hesitation, at 22% (slide 18), and brands now test before and after supplements (photo 4). Science published behind the scenes "will feed all the AI tools" consumers ask for advice [00:04]. My reading: brands will ask suppliers for clinical evidence and outcomes a consumer can measure; our evidence should be ready, public and easy for those tools to read.
- Relevance high: consumer data on ageing, with energy and strength as the leading concern and proteins named by one in five.

  - Women list emotional wellbeing first at 18 to 24 and weight first at 25 to 34; mobility, joint and bone health comes first in every band from 35 to 44 up. Cognitive decline appears at 55 to 64 and loss of independence at 65 plus.
  - Weight appears in two men's and three women's bands; chronic diseases in three men's bands and one women's.
  - In the deck the chart is partly behind a text box; its legend names energy, mobility, weight management and chronic diseases (slide 8).
- What products must show, per the slide: energy and physical strength; mobility, joint and bone health; weight management; cognitive performance; everyday activity and recovery (slide 8). As she said it: "energy and physical strength, mobility, joint health, weight management, cognitive, and everyday activity support and recovery" [00:04].
- Niagen, which Otter heard as "Niagara": the slide reads "How Niagen reinvented itself: from product to purpose, from a supplement brand into a longevity platform". It redefined the market from "NAD+ supplements" to "healthy aging and longevity"; added Niagen Plus telehealth, Niagen IV and NAD+ injections; took NAD+ into topical skincare with NanoCloud; and is building a drug pipeline (NB4168, for rare diseases and ageing-related conditions). "Consumers do not buy nicotinamide riboside. They buy energy, vitality and a longer healthspan." Source: Niagen's investor presentation, November 2026. The slide repeats Niagen's line that NAD+ declines by up to about 65% between 30 and 70 (slide 9). Her "500 studies" and "100 patents", as heard, are not on the slide [00:04].
- Single most important to long-term health goals, by life stage (the darker bars; the lighter bars carry no label):
  - UK women, late 30s: mental wellbeing 20%, sleep 20% (circled), reducing stress 14%, healthy eating 12%, exercise 11%, weight management 6%, metabolic health 5%, gut health 3%, preventative medical testing 3%, supplements 3%. Message: "Cellular energy, cell renewal, mitochondrial health, re-energise your cells, cellular decline starts in 30s" (slide 10).
  - UK women, late 40s: mental wellbeing 19%, exercise 15%, sleep 14%, weight management 14%, healthy eating 13%, reducing stress 11%, gut health 5%, muscle mass/strength 5%, metabolic health 3%; weight, exercise, gut and muscle are circled. Message: "Supports cellular cardiovascular health, muscles, counteract oestrogen decline" (slide 11).
  - Italian women, late 40s: mental wellbeing 19%, healthy eating 13%, sleep 5%, metabolic health 4%, gut health 2%; preventative medical testing is third on the list, its value hidden. Message: "Test your levels… repeat tests after supplementation" (slide 12). She said "The previous data was for the UK and Italy" [00:04].
  - US men, late 30s: sleep 23% (circled), exercise 22%, healthy eating 14%, reducing stress 13%, mental wellbeing 9%, weight management 9%, preventative medical testing 3%, metabolic health 3%, gut health 2%, supplements 2%. Message: "Cellular energy, muscle support, biohacking" (slide 13).
  - US men, late 40s: healthy eating 21% (circled), exercise 17%, mental wellbeing 13%, sleep 12%, reducing stress 9%, supplements 7% (circled), weight management 5%, preventative medical testing 5%, gut health 5%, muscle mass/strength 2%, metabolic health 2%. Message: "Age better, double the dose to counteract for natural loss" (slide 14). She said healthy eating "really over-indexes" for men ten years on and they are "much more so into supplements" [00:04].
- GLP-1 users in the UK, habits since starting treatment, top three: increased significantly, interest in healthy foods 68%, exercise frequency 61%, interest in preventative health 61%; decreased significantly, alcohol 64%, eating and drinking out of home 57%, snacking 50% (slide 15). Otter heard the second increase as "increase longevity" [00:04]; the slide says exercise frequency.
- Lumina's UK GLP-1 tracker is the GLP-Navigator, on GLP-1's impact on UK out-of-home consumption. Almost 27% of the UK population, about 18.4 million people, currently use (6.1%), have used (5.7%) or are considering (15.1%) GLP-1 drugs (slide 16).
- 36% ("1 in 3") take supplements specifically to counteract natural ageing (slide 17). Ingredient categories seen as most helpful for extending healthspan: vitamins 50%, omega-3 39%, minerals 25%, probiotics 22%, antioxidants and polyphenols 21%, prebiotics and fibre 21%, amino acids and proteins 20%, not sure 13%, CoQ10 8%, botanical extracts 7%, postbiotics 5% (slide 17). The slide names no country. On postbiotics, Nick Stene of Euromonitor gave US share growth of 48% and a price index of 2.83 (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan); consumer belief here is 5%. The two measure different things; both are given.
- Biggest hesitation about longevity supplements, UK: not enough proof 22%, cost 21%, don't believe claims 20%, safety concerns 20%, too many options 10%, remembering to take them 7%, other 1% (slide 18).
- Life Extension's ageing tests on photo 4: Phenotypic Age Project Panel blood test USD 105.00 ("Test key aging markers and calculate biological age"); Healthy Aging Panel (Comprehensive) USD 249.00; Healthy Aging Panel (Basic) USD 155.00; MTHFR/COMT genetic methylation cheek swab USD 149.00 (photo 4). She gave the biological-age blood test as "for $100" [00:04].
- Novos, confirmed: the deck's version of the slide adds a novoslabs.com screenshot of NOVOS Age, an at-home finger-prick test said to return biological age, pace of ageing, the ages of 11 organs and systems, and telomere length; one kit USD 349, or USD 299 each for two or more; ships within the US and Canada. Its caption: "How do we help people manage the rate at which they age? Supplement brand → Health intelligence company" (slide 19). Photo 4 shows an earlier build without it. In the talk she called Novos "Another similar example" [00:04].
- Her reading of test and retest: it shows a brand's trust in its ingredients, a positive result may make the most loyal consumers, and it is "a way of going around the health legislation a little bit" because "whatever is on the back is becoming less relevant" [00:04].
- "the health plan leaders of the next decade may not be the pure product companies themselves", but platforms "that measure, manage, and optimize aging" [00:04]. The slide says "healthspan leaders" and adds "Applied & communicated science number 1 trust creator" (slide 19).
- NutraIngredients Europe Awards entries by category, 2022 to 2026: ingredients for healthspan rise from about 16 entries to about 30, ahead of mind and mood (about 23) and beauty from within (about 20) in 2026, read from the chart (slide 20). The slide carries a "The Grocer Health Summit 2026" tag. Otter heard the category as "health fund" [00:04].
- Winners and finalists for Ingredient of the Year in those three categories include Niagen, Affron, Zeropollution, Levagen, Cognizin Citicoline, CurQfen, HydroCurc, SR CarnoSyn sustained-release beta-alanine and an HMB with vitamin D3 entry; none of our ingredients is among the readable names (slide 21).
- She closed with consumers' hopes for wellness technology in 2040 ("All cancers cured", "Portable lungs") and a quote from Jonas Salk [00:04] (slide 22). Her five conclusions: a generational shift to prevention; consumers reinventing themselves; suppliers and brands moving from product to platform; GLP-1s accelerating healthier behaviours; trust as "the industry's biggest challenge and biggest opportunity" (slide 23).

files.name: otter-summary.md
files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Recording: "Ewa Hudson - Healthspan", https://otter.ai/u/cIf3E0sDizFN1GEBbAdmh0a8sAs, 10 Nov 2026, 17m 42s.

## Summary

Ewa Hudson presents insights on the generational shift in longevity aspirations and the evolving role of the healthspan industry.

## Consumer Trends
**Generational Shifts**
* Younger populations view healthy aging as a preventative opportunity rather than a reactive one. 
* While 39% of those aged 65+ believe genetics play a major role in aging, only 21% of younger respondents share this view.
* Interest in supplements is higher among younger cohorts; 20% of the 25–34 age group believe in their efficacy compared to only 12% of those over 65.
* Aging well is increasingly defined by vitality and the ability to reinvent oneself, exemplified by rising numbers of entrepreneurs over age 50 and extreme athletes.

**Demographic Needs**
* **Energy and Stamina**: Identified as the top health concern for both men and women across all age brackets.
* **Gender Specifics**: Women prioritize mobility, joint health, and bone health, while men focus heavily on exercise and healthy eating as they age.
* **Age-Specific Drivers**: For women in their late 30s, sleep is a primary concern, whereas weight management and muscle strength become more critical ten years later.

## Industry Evolution
**Business Models**
* Companies are transitioning from product-focused entities to purpose-driven service platforms. Examples include **Niagara**, which moved into IV injections and pharma-adjacent spaces, and **Life Extension**, which offers biological age blood tests to allow consumers to track supplement efficacy through data.
* **Novos** is repositioning itself from a supplement brand to a "health intelligence company."

**Challenges and Opportunities**
* **The Trust Gap**: The primary hesitation for consumers regarding longevity supplements is "not enough proof," signaling a need for increased scientific validation.
* **Technological Integration**: AI tools like **ChatGPT** are becoming central to how consumers seek personalized advice, necessitating that brands provide high-quality scientific data to feed these models.
* **GLP-1 Impact**: The rise of **GLP-1** treatments is shifting consumer behaviors toward healthier food choices, increased interest in longevity, and decreased alcohol consumption.

How can companies better bridge the trust gap through applied science? How will the rise of AI-driven personal planning reshape supplement marketing?

## Action items

- Speaker 0 - : Arrange a date for the 30-year marathon challenge for interested participants who speak with her.
- Stephen Daniells (NutraIngredients) - : Invite the panelists onto the stage.
- Speaker 0 - : Arrange the date for the 30-year marathon challenge.

detail.text: Billing: Ewa Hudson, Strategy & Insight Director, ReThink Global, under the Lumina Intelligence name (slide 1); the closing slide says "Strategy & Insights Director" (slide 24). Lumina is part of the William Reed group, which also runs NutraIngredients and this summit (slide 25). No slide is marked Confidential.
The whole talk is one Otter turn starting at [00:04], labelled Speaker 1; Stephen Daniells (NutraIngredients) thanks her at [17:12].

Survey base: carried out in July 2026, n=10,500, in Brazil, China, France, Germany, Italy, Saudi Arabia, Spain, the UK and the USA (slide 1); 2,000 in China, 1,250 each in the US and Brazil, 1,000 in each other country (slide 23). She said "over 10,000 people in nine countries" [00:04]. The ninth country, cut off on photo 3, is the USA (slide 8). The full report is offered for download by QR code (slide 23).
Her three parts: longevity aspirations across generations, what consumers want and need, and whether scientific innovation on its own is enough to earn consumers' trust [00:04].

Genetics as a big factor in extending healthspan, all countries: 39% at 65 plus, 31% at 55 to 64, 26% at 45 to 54, 24% at 35 to 44, 23% at 25 to 34, 21% at 18 to 24 (slide 2), as she said them [00:04]. She added 50% in Italy and Saudi Arabia, which the deck does not show [00:04]. The slide: exercise, sleep and diet "play biggest impact" (slide 2).

Supplements as having an impact: 20% at 25 to 34, 19% at 35 to 44, 17% at 45 to 64, 12% at 65 plus (slide 3), as she said them [00:04]; the deck gives no figure for 18 to 24. She linked the 12% to retired people starting to think about ageing in their 60s [00:04].
Age of first serious thought about ageing, two builds of one chart:

Photo 1 shows the Retired series: 1% (20s), 3% (30s), 10% (40s), 27% (50s), 36% (60s), 11% (70s), and 10% have not started (photo 1). With those values the Retired bars and "have not started" come to about 100%, so the 27% belongs to the Retired bar (my reading).

The deck (slide 4) shows the same chart with "Working full-time" as the labelled series: 10% (50s), 2% (60s), 10% have not started. The 20s, 30s and 40s are behind a text box; read from the chart, about 24%, 30% and 24% (slide 4).

The lighter bars carry no label in the photo or the deck; they are the same in both builds (read from the charts). The slide's message: "Healthy aging is seen as a PREVENTATIVE OPPORTUNITY" (slide 4).

Ageing goals: 52% want to age slowly and healthily, 16% to prevent premature ageing, 11% to reverse ageing (photo 2) (slide 5). She added "another 18% want to stay just as they are", which neither the photo nor the deck shows [00:04].

Ambition with age, as Otter heard it: a US Census study of 2.7 million founders found the fastest-growing 0.1% of new ventures were founded at 45 on average, and a 50-year-old was "roughly 1.1 times as likely" as a 30-year-old to found an exceptional-growth company [00:04]. The slide shows a Business Matters headline of 12 March 2024, "Huge boom in over 50 year old entrepreneurs with Start Up Loans providing over £140m of finance", and links to a census study of high-growth founders' average age and an American Economic Review: Insights paper (slide 6).

Late-life runners: she said runners who took up running in their 70s, 80s and 90s run marathons at 100 [00:04]. summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired two retailers, a brand and a marketplace: Jessica Pasco of Holland & Barrett, Rachel Kreider of GNC, Federico Luna of Timeline and Jennifer Wang of Alibaba's Taobao Tmall. His question: is longevity a real category, or an umbrella for outcomes consumers already understand?

They agreed that shoppers pay for benefits they can feel or see. Prevention alone is hard to sell, so proof and a tangible result, such as stronger muscles or better skin, matter most. They also agreed that GLP-1 medicines move people into a proactive mindset, and that creatine and muscle are a way into healthy ageing.

They differed on the category itself. Luna said longevity is absolutely a category, defined by the hallmarks of ageing and four pillars, and that bundling a generic vitamin C into it does consumers a disservice. Pasco said Holland & Barrett's new in-store longevity category is small but growing fast, driven mainly by NAD, while most proactive shopping is not badged longevity. Kreider said GNC treats healthy ageing as a demand space and links new ingredients to condition-specific products. Wang said nobody in China searches for longevity online: men search for sexual vitality and women for sagging skin, and premium shoppers ask for patents and clinical studies.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Holland & Barrett created a longevity category in store over the last six months; it is "still quite small" but has seen "really significant growth", driven primarily by NAD, with spermidine less popular [02:58] [03:47].
- GNC defines healthy ageing as a target demand space and is extending its condition-specific preventive nutrition brand into standalone longevity ingredients such as NAD+; Kreider said consumers need to connect it to a benefit they can feel [08:44].
- Online in China, longevity is not a search term: the trigger for men is sexual vitality and for women sagging skin, followed by joints, sleep and metabolism [06:09].
- GLP-1 as a gateway: Pasco sees customers entering the category because they start a GLP-1 journey and staying after they stop the medication [14:52]; Kreider sees an opportunity for products that protect muscle on that journey [15:59].
- Creatine is crossing over: Kreider said people engage with healthy ageing through creatine and active nutrition, and Pasco said creatine is "moving from a more of a sports focus into this longevity space" [17:19] [19:15].
- Proof decides the role of an ingredient: Kreider wants hero ingredients with clinical substantiation and a tangible benefit, with buzzier ingredients as background [31:12]; Wang said Chinese shoppers ask for a branded ingredient, a patent and a clinical study, and pay the premium [22:45].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Two major retailers, GNC and Holland & Barrett, both see creatine moving from sports into healthy ageing [17:19] [19:15]. My reading: CreaWin can be pitched to healthy-ageing ranges, on its own evidence for muscle.
- GLP-1 users are entering the supplement aisle and staying, and muscle protection is the named need [14:52] [15:59]. My reading: protein and creatine for muscle on a GLP-1 journey are a pitch retailers already recognise.
- Retailers want hero ingredients with clinical substantiation and a benefit the shopper can feel [08:44] [31:12]. My reading: our pitches to healthy-ageing brands should lead with a felt outcome and the study behind it, not a mechanism.
- Chinese premium shoppers ask for branded ingredients, patents and studies, and Chinese brands combine several branded ingredients in one product [22:45]. My reading: Tmall cross-border is a channel where branded, documented ingredients earn their price.
- Relevance high: retailer category structure for healthy ageing, creatine and GLP-1 muscle.
