# Clicks to Community: Turning Digital Engagement into Brand Loyalty: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "SNS Panel - digital engagement", https://otter.ai/u/AFcS0eaniyWZMj-cu4IFkai0za0, recorded 9 Nov 2026 09:54, 40m 27s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:01] Speaker 1: Discover, evaluate, and purchase wellness products today. However, a recent report that we reported on at NI showed that there are more than 1,000 misleading food communication posts by influencers online with supplements the most frequent subject matter. So, while there's a huge opportunity to use social media to create communities, and really it's it's an essential part of brand strategy today, the industry is very much being watched carefully. And so with that, I'd like to just start the discussion with the brands that we have here on stage, because we have Shanae from Tonic and Julian from AG One, which are both huge online, massive online followings, but very different communication strategies. Both of your brands. So first of all, Sinead, would you give us a brief description of Tonic's online com strategy, and what is it about Tonic's content that makes people
[01:00] Speaker 2: stop scrolling? Yeah, sure. Thanks, Nikki. So, our kind of objective with our content is to make sure that everything that we do educates and just doesn't sell anything. So, we have flagship content which is called the Unsponsored Truth. So, Sunner, our founder of Tonic, goes around supermarkets and gives people in simple, realistic, healthy swaps that they can make in their everyday life to make themselves healthier. We've been running the content for about four years now, so we now have 1.9 million followers on social, and we get about 70 million views every single month, which, for a brand our size, is just insane and it's unheard of, and yeah, it's just incredible to have that kind of support from our community. I would say why our content works is because it's so simple, easy, and actionable. So you know, we kind of run the kind of brand now as a media business that happens to sell vitamins rather than actually what we are is we are a vitamin brand that essentially has overnight or not overnight the last four years I would say has just built this kind of following and you know vitamins came first and the kind of media is just what built the brand I would say you know why people engage with our content is probably because it's genuinely useful. It's 20 to 32nd clips. We post three times a day. We're educating you on just how to make one simple switch in your life to make yourself healthier. And I think from a kind of social perspective, people go to social for two things and two things only, and that is to be educated or to be entertained. And if you're not doing either of those two things as a brand, then you're gonna fail on social, frankly. And I think we've managed to just hit the nail on the head with kind of that education piece and give people simple, easy tricks that they can just take away into their everyday life. And I think why it works so well for us is because essentially we have a brand mission to expose the truth, expose the lies, build truth within the category to help people thrive. So every piece of content we do kind of sits within in that umbrella, and I think just genuinely be useful to people's lives is kind of why why you will like succeed?
[03:21] Speaker 1: Yeah. So key tip: don't try and sell your product.
[03:24] Speaker 2: Don't sell your product. Yeah. I mean, 99% of our content is not about our product, which a lot of people on our board and you know investors constantly question every day. And we stand by it because we bring people in a funnel, and as soon as they are ready to purchase a vitamin, they might ask us what the best vitamin is, or when they might get to the kind of supermarket shelf, they might look at the vitamin category and be like, "Oh, actually, I follow tonic. Let me just try theirs." But we're very, very soft and educational, and we yeah, I think 0.01% of our content is actually about our vitamins. Interesting. And so then
[04:00] Speaker 1: Julian, a key part of AG1's USP is the scientific backing, but science is notoriously difficult to try and communicate to someone in a social media post. So, how do you get around that? How much of your communication is about the research backing of the product?
[04:17] Speaker 3: So, we started by talking a lot about it, we talked a lot about our, you know, Goldstone, the clinical trials. We talked a lot about the the volume of third-party testing that we have in like all of our core markets, from the US to Europe to the UK to Australia, and people didn't care. And you know, Sinead has actually hit the nail on the head. Where people, particularly in a social environment, they come to be educated or entertained. But I would say with education that the key is to make it hyper relevant to that specific person to speak in their language, to understand what is the trigger point for them wanting to be interested in anything connected to to preventative health, which is something that's going to improve their lives, our mission has always been to empower people to take ownership of their health. So it's about figuring out what are the ways in which we can like give people the kind of the evidence they need to go after it. And what we've learned over time is, particularly a top of funnel, particularly in social. Too much evidence doesn't work. You know, we launch campaigns around in the US around WTF is NSF, NSF being the biggest kind of sports thing. We you know we did we did campaigns specifically about that on YouTube. We have a series called Dropping Hours, which is about trying to humanize this idea of all of the science that goes into our products, and that that has been quite successful. Again, because we're not selling anything, we're just providing information. But ultimately, social is about sparking curiosity, and it's about driving an association between a brand that has credibility to know what it's talking about without making the consumer necessarily do the work of like figuring out what does a gold standard clinical trial actually mean. You know, we need to make it relevant for them.
[06:11] Speaker 1: Okay, brilliant. And so, along the similar lines, then Dan, I'm interested to to know your point of view as a nutritionist. What would be your tips for how to simplify, perhaps simplify science or get across complicated messages or claims in a in a post?
[06:30] Speaker 4: Yeah, I think often when we think of the role of a nutritionist within a brand, it used to be very much like ambassador based, and you know certainly me being in the industry 10 years used to be very much kind of people wanting to offer commission or offer benefits for somebody to post the product and kind of just shout about how great it's. I think now with the emerging research and all of the different kind of I suppose angles that you can take on socials, whether that be like we said entertainment or kind of education. I think you know a nutritionist plays a big role in translating that information to the day-to-day consumer, working across professional sports myself, I find often that you know athletes don't really want the numbers, or you know you can shout as much as you want about the numbers. And as you were saying, you know certain things that you're doing in clinical trials, but what they want is the headline. But also to ensure that that's backed by the research. I think it's a really careful way of doing it because often I'll work with brands individually or as a as a business, and they'll want to put out some quite outlandish claims based on their their research. And sometimes you have to pull them back and say, you know, it's it's great that we can post about that on social media, but let's take the angle which ultimately the consumer is going to understand, and also that we're using the research to its best effect. I think there's a a lot of brands out there that maybe don't have that advisory from a nutritionist within industry that often will take a research paper or a cluster of research papers and want to use that directly with their brand and almost use the research to fit their mold, as opposed to using the research for what the intended purpose was. I think often a nutritionist not just navigates how to get it across to consumers, but can help them to navigate that research piece as well. Of how do we take genuine research and turn it into actionable insights and claims across social media?
[08:18] Speaker 1: Yeah, and you've touched on it a little bit there, perhaps, but I wanted to ask you what are some of the red flags, signs of when brands are not communicating science or health claims in the most transparent way?
[08:33] Speaker 4: How old we got? No, I think often you know a lot of the times it's it's the use of certain words that maybe don't present in the research because the words within the research are considered a little bit too dull or boring to present on social media. But the connotation of the words very different, and I think that's what really kind of trips me up when I'm looking at branding. Is they're using certain buzzwords that they know will get reaction because they potentially ran it through an AI model, for example, and it said this is the best kind of trending word that you can use. When actually the connotations can be very different, and I think often it comes out of like genuine accidental misleading, as opposed to like genuine trying to mislead a consumer. But I think it's it's the wording often that I think trips up a lot of brands is you know what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area, and it's not really you know regulated well. But I think you know as nutritionists, we can do a lot better job with brands to help them to communicate the message effectively.
[09:32] Speaker 1: Brilliant, thank you. And so Luca, to bring you in to talk about the regulations that are in play here, what are some of the key rules that marketers need to be aware of when they're marketing their products online.
[09:45] Luca Buccini (ESSNA): So thank you, Nikki. I think there are many rules now, and more are coming because, as you heard, marketing online is essential to communicate to consumers, to educate consumers. That's where our consumers, athletes, consumers go for information, go for education. So it's essential to be there, and regulators, regulators catching up. So we do have rules. We have rules about product communication, quite restrictive, nutrition and health claims regulation, which is very so that's the first piece of regulation in the UK. You have all the codes by the Advertising Authority. That that's really the most essential context in practice. And the other member states of the EU, the member states of the EU, have their own scenarios on influencer marketing and so on. So you have to check them as well. So that's very important. We have new pieces of regulations coming, and the Digital Finance Act. We don't know the text yet, but it's coming. So I think the overall effect of the current situation, which we have been communicating on social media, it has created tensions within teams, especially regulatory teams and marketing teams, all the time. And I think you know, if you are in our society, has has regulation held how how how the industry back? No, no, it's been a great way to communicate to communicate social media, increasing the AI as well. But I think there's been problems with the level playing field. Companies, especially responsible brands, have had to navigate that space. summary.Summary:
Nikki Hancocks of NutraIngredients chaired a panel on how brands build communities online while regulators watch. She opened with a report of more than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers, with supplements the most frequent subject.

The panel agreed that social content works when it educates or entertains rather than sells. Sinead Gibbons said almost none of Tonic Health's content is about its products; its supermarket swap videos have built 1.9 million followers. Julian Harvie said AG1 learned that talking about its trials and testing did not land, so it keeps the science further down the funnel and practises restraint; Clearcast rejected three versions of its TV advert's opening line. Dan Richardson, a nutritionist in professional sport, said athletes want the headline backed by research, that brands slip by using buzzwords whose meaning differs from the research, and that athletes are the most impressionable audience of all.

Luca Bucchini, speaking for ESSNA, set out the rules and the failures he sees most: undisclosed ads, and marketing strategies built around non-compliance. Brands carry most of the responsibility for what their influencers claim. On AI, Julian's rule is that every idea begins and ends with a human; Luca expects regulators to act as people take nutrition advice from AI.
summary.Key takeaways:
- More than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].
- Tonic runs itself as "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 99% of its content is not about its products, and it has 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month [01:00], [03:24].
- AG1 found that talking about trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel; the science sits mid-funnel [04:17], [18:30].
- Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
- Brands bear most responsibility for their influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
- Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": they believe a claim of "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Our customers' marketing teams are under claims pressure from the ASA, Clearcast and the claims regulation, and the panel's answer was education that does not sell: "what is creatine, how does it work" is exactly what AG1 makes with its experts [22:46].
- My reading: a branded ingredient earns its place by giving brands substantiated, claim-safe education they can publish, in the headline-plus-evidence form Dan described, not by giving them stronger claims [06:30].
- For CreaWin, Dan's food-first framing and his athlete stories show creatine is already a mainstay for athletes and nutritionists [24:22], [32:33]. My reading: our creatine content should be calm and educational, and wording we supply to brands must survive an ASA review.
- Brands carry the liability for what influencers say [28:27]. My reading: they will want suppliers' claims referenced and hedged exactly.
- Relevance medium: marketing and regulation, adjacent to our ingredients.

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Industry experts discussed effective digital engagement strategies, regulatory compliance, and the role of science in social media marketing for wellness brands.

## Content Strategy
**Sinead** from **Tonic** explained that their strategy focuses on education rather than direct selling, utilizing a "media business" model to build community. By providing simple, actionable health swaps through flagship content like **Unsponsored Truth**, they have reached 1.9 million followers and 70 million monthly views. **Julian** from **AG1** noted that while scientific evidence is a USP, too much technical detail fails on social media; instead, they focus on humanizing science through series like **Dropping Hours** to spark curiosity.

**Dan**, a nutritionist, highlighted the importance of translating complex research into "headlines" that consumers can understand. He warned against using buzzwords or AI-generated language that may have different connotations than the original research, potentially leading to accidental misinformation.

## Regulatory Compliance
**Luca** from **ESSNA** outlined the complexities of navigating UK **Advertising Authority** codes and varying EU member state regulations regarding influencer marketing. He identified several key risks:
* Failure to disclose paid advertisements or partnerships.
* Marketing strategies built around non-compliance rather than adherence to rules.
* Brands following non-compliant discourse trends seen in comment sections.

**Sinead** shared a specific misstep where a social media manager used an unreviewed claim ("best sleep supplement") on a profile cover, resulting in an **ASA** intervention. To prevent this, **Tonic** now uses an **AI** agent to review content for compliance. **Julian** also discussed the difficulty of working with creative agencies like **Clearcast**, noting how strict regulations forced a shift from "best version of you" to more compliant messaging in TV commercials.

## Future Trends
The panel addressed the impact of **AI** on the industry:
* **Julian** argued that while **AI** helps scale content, human insight must remain at both the beginning and end of the creative process to ensure quality and empathy.
* **Luca** suggested that regulators will likely introduce new rules as **AI** agents begin to provide personalized nutritional advice and visual information.
* **Dan** observed that athletes remain highly impressionable, often seeking a competitive edge through unverified claims found on platforms like **TikTok Shop**.

How will upcoming regulations like the **Digital Finance Act** specifically impact the intersection of **AI** and nutrition marketing?

Action items (as returned):
- Speaker 2 - : Ensure AI-assisted content begins with a human consumer insight and ends with human review and rewriting, using AI only to help scale or refine content in the middle of the process.
- Speaker 2 - : Maintain a human-in-the-loop content process: start each AI-assisted message with a human insight, use AI only for intermediate scaling or refinement, and finish with human review and rewriting.

detail.text: Tonic's flagship content is the "Unsponsored Truth": its founder gives simple supermarket swaps. Clips are 20 to 30 seconds, three posts a day; people come to social "to be educated or to be entertained" [01:00], [03:24].

Tonic posts 900 pieces of content a month across four channels with one 22-year-old social media manager and a freelance editor. After the ASA pulled up a profile cover for its magnesium drink ("...she wrote on the social cover the best sleep supplement in the market, and now we don't have that claim"), every piece now goes through an AI compliance agent [14:35].
Tonic never deletes a challenged post: it changes the caption, answers the comments, sends voice notes and makes response videos, because "trust is really built in those small moments" [14:35].

Julian: on social, people "come to be educated or entertained", and education must be hyper relevant to the person; "Too much evidence doesn't work." AG1's US campaign "WTF is NSF" and its "Dropping Hours" series humanise the science without selling [04:17].

AG1 cannot associate healthcare professionals, dietitians or doctors directly with the brand, so it uses them for pure education ("what is creatine? Like, how does it work?", "why is magnesium important?") and hopes the credibility transfers [22:46].

Dan: athletes want the headline, backed by the research. The common slip is swapping dull research words for buzzwords whose connotations differ, often "genuine accidental misleading"; "what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area" [06:30], [08:33].
Dan is food first: on a creatine company's podcast he said not everybody should take creatine until the baseline of nutrition is fixed, and the company objected [24:22].

Luca's rules: the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules, and a new digital act whose text is not yet known (Otter: "Digital Finance Act") [09:45].
Luca's recurring failures: undisclosed ads, no training or allocated responsibility with creators, strategies built around non-compliance, and following a non-compliant discourse [11:59].
Provocation without a solution is fearmongering: Tonic will not post a call-out unless it gives the healthier swap [30:18].

AI: Julian's hard rule is that "...the idea has to begin and end with a human being"; AI scales the middle, and he found human copy still better by some margin [35:43]. summary.Summary:
Dr Emily Jevons, a registered nutritionist who specialises in sports nutrition, nutrition education and disordered eating, asked how much of women's sports nutrition is science and how much is myth.

She began with the evidence base. Only 6% of sport and exercise science publications study women alone. Even when women are included, their hormonal status is rarely verified properly. Women are not one population either: adolescents, contraceptive users, pregnant and postpartum women and women in menopause all differ, and the last groups are almost absent from research.

On the menstrual cycle she was clear. Most studies find no effect of cycle phase on performance; effects are small and individual variation is large. Popular advice to train hard early in the cycle and switch to pilates later is not backed by the evidence. Carbohydrate needs follow the training session, not the phase. Energy availability comes first; in theory, protein needs may rise in the luteal phase.

She then turned to the women's health aisle, where demand is outpacing evidence, and asked whether it is pink washing or progress. Her answer for industry: use ingredients with evidence for the outcome claimed, at trial doses, fully disclosed and batch-tested; claim honestly; design with women; and fund female-specific trials, publishing null results too.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The evidence gap: of 5,261 publications with 12,511,386 participants, 63% studied males and females, 31% males only and 6% females only (Cowley et al., 2021) (slide 4).
- Even when women are included, 14% of performance supplement studies defined menstrual status and about 0.5% verified it with best-practice methods; female participation rose from about 39% (2011-13) to about 44% (2021-23) (Smith et al., 2022; Ose et al., 2025) (slide 6).
- The cycle and performance: 13 of 16 studies found no effect on anaerobic performance and 14 of 22 none on aerobic performance; no influence of phase on strength or training adaptations, "BUT motivation could be impactful" (Carmichael et al., 2021; Colenso-Semple et al., 2023). A review found the evidence does not warrant general guidance on changing exercise across the cycle (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 15) (slide 16).
- Nutrition: carbohydrate targets are per kg of body mass and apply to both sexes, with no evidence for phase-specific targets; energy intake tends to rise about 170 kcal a day in the luteal phase. The primary focus is adequate energy intake and optimal energy availability (ISSN position stand, Sims et al., 2023) (slide 18) (slide 19).
- Protein: high-quality protein as close to the start and/or end of exercise as possible at 0.3-0.4 g/kg body weight, aiming for the upper end in the luteal phase "due to the catabolic actions of progesterone" (Sims et al., 2023) (slide 20).
- Building better products: include only ingredients with evidence for the outcome claimed, "e.g. creatine 3–5 g/day alongside strength training for midlife muscle and strength"; use trial doses, list every dose, batch-test for athletes (e.g. Informed Sport); use authorised claims; co-design with women and fund female-specific studies (slide 23).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: her one named example of an evidence-based ingredient for women was creatine, 3-5 g a day alongside strength training for midlife muscle and strength (slide 23). My reading: this is the CreaWin case for women in a nutritionist's own words, and it rests on trials, so our material should lead with trial doses and references.
- Women's creatine products are already on the shelf. Her slides show Zooki Creatine+ for Women (5 g creatine, "extra support for energy, cognition and hormonal balance") and Marchon Women's Formula (5 g creatine, 4 g myo-inositol, 8 g marine collagen), read from the pack shots, under "Cycle syncing, myth or evidence based?" and "Pink washing or progress?"; she gave no verdict on each product (slide 11) (slide 21). My reading: "hormonal balance" is the kind of claim she warns against (slide 23); a brand that wants her kind of approval needs trial-dose creatine and honest claims, which is where CreaWin should sit.
- Protein: 0.3-0.4 g/kg around exercise (slide 20). My reading: about 18-24 g a serving for a 60 kg woman, a dose a clear pea protein drink (IsoClr: Pea) can carry.
- Her industry list asks for female-specific trials with verified menstrual status, research on the product not just the ingredient, and published null results (slide 24). My reading: a CreaWin study in active women designed that way would answer her directly, and she asks for nutritionists to be involved "from day one" (slide 23).
- James Morton (SiS) said the same at 11:20: fuel for the work, not the menstrual cycle (fuelling-the-female-runner-from-paper). SiS is among the logos on her "Who am I?" slide (slide 2).
summary.Quotes:
- "Hormones treated as noise: the cycle was seen as a confounder to avoid rather than a variable to study." (slide 5)
- "Carbohydrate needs are driven by the training session, not the cycle phase." (slide 18)
- "Demand is outpacing evidence" (slide 22)
- "Women's products should be built on evidence, not trends." (slide 25)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm the end time, track, her organisation and role as billed, and the programme title.
- Talk to Emily Jevons (contact details on slides 1 and 26) about what a CreaWin study in active or midlife women should look like; she named creatine 3-5 g a day as her evidence-based example (slide 23).
- Find the papers: Cowley et al. 2021, Smith et al. 2022, Ose et al. 2025, McNulty et al. 2020, Carmichael et al. 2021, Colenso-Semple et al. 2023, the ISSN female athlete position stand (Sims et al. 2023) and the UCL 2026 review of menopause supplements.
- Find out who supplies the creatine in Zooki Creatine+ for Women and Marchon Women's Formula (slide 11) (slide 21).
summary.Detail:
- Why research leaned on men: the "70 kg male" became the reference participant; hormones were treated as noise; testing women properly means verifying phase with hormone measures across several phases; contraception variety makes uniform groups harder; product claims were built on male evidence, "This is where industry can now lead" (slide 5).
- Women aren't one population: adolescents; menstruating women with a natural cycle; women on hormonal contraception, which suppresses endogenous hormones and may be used to manage conditions such as endometriosis; pregnancy and postpartum, a one to two year period; peri- and menopause, diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without menstruation. "Lots of individual variation across all phases" (slide 7). The hormone curves across the lifespan are marked "Illustrative – not to scale" (slide 8).
- About 50% of elite athletes use hormonal contraception (Martin et al. 2018); 77% of non-users report negative cycle symptoms, mostly on days 1-2 of bleeding; peri- and postmenopausal athletes are almost absent from research; adolescents, pregnancy and postpartum have even less data; findings in one group can't simply be applied to another (slide 9).
- She asked the room "Who is your target audience?" before the cycle-syncing section (slide 10). The cycle-syncing slide also shows an SiS Run Fuel gel and Fast and Female (slide 11).
- Physiology: the 28-day cycle is an average, not a rule; the follicular phase is the more variable; the luteal phase lasts about 12-15 days after ovulation; the LH surge is not exactly day 14; stress, sleep, body weight, training load and life context all affect the pattern (slide 12). "Every woman will experience the menstrual cycle differently" (slide 13).
- Proposed mechanisms. Muscle activation: in theory oestrogen raises excitability and progesterone "may lower strength outcomes in the luteal phase". Muscle and tendon stiffness: oestrogen may change collagen synthesis, but "Most research states this increase is not great enough to have an effect". Thermoregulation: a sufficient warm-up nulled any luteal advantage; higher body temperature could hurt endurance. Metabolism: trends disappear at higher intensities or when fed; exercise intensity and nutrition status appear "to be more influential than menstrual cycle phase" (slide 14).
- One study found peak power higher in the ovulatory phase, but motivation to train was also greatest then; intermittent endurance is more likely to be affected than continuous endurance (slide 15).
- What social media says (crossed out on the slide): train hard early, pilates and walking later. What the review says: performance "might be reduced by a small amount" in the early phase, with large personal differences (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 16). Her conclusion: a personalised approach based on each woman's response (slide 17).
- Resting metabolic rate may rise slightly in the luteal phase, but studies are inconsistent and mostly low quality; combined pill users do not show these fluctuations (slide 18).
- Protein: oestrogen is anabolic and progesterone catabolic, so in theory an athletic woman might need more protein in the luteal phase, but rising metabolic rate and appetite are already likely to raise her intake (slide 20).
- The women's health aisle: UK menopause supplements projected to grow from £42m (2020) to £100m by 2028 (GenM/Kantar); Holland & Barrett women's health sales up 22% year on year; a UCL 2026 review found half of UK menopause supplements had no vitamin D and only 24% contained calcium; "hormone balance" stacks (DIM, inositol, vitex, ashwagandha) are booming online (slide 22).
- Packs on the "Pink washing or progress?" slide, read from the pack shots: Wassen Prime Protect 50+ Women, Hairburst Womens 35+ Hair Vitamins (with added collagen), Viviscal, Swedish Collagen Collagen Deluxe (12,500 mg hydrolysed marine collagen), Novomins Women's Bio-Balance Gummies and Zooki Creatine+ for Women (slide 21).
- The four rules in full: Justify (no trending "oestrogen balance" ingredients without evidence in active women); Dose and Disclose (no proprietary blends at token doses, untested for banned substances); Claim honestly (no "balances your hormones" or "cycle-synced" without trials; say what isn't yet known); Co-design (not "a pink tub on the same formula") (slide 23).
- What industry can do: fund female-specific trials rather than adding women to male designs; verify menstrual status with best-practice methods, not day-counting; educate on who the product is for; research the product, not just the ingredient; publish null results (slide 24).
- Take-home messages: more high-quality research across the lifespan; cycle effects small, individual variation large, energy availability first; products built on evidence; industry can fund, design and report better research (slide 25).
- Her "Who am I?" slide carries logos including SiS, British Cycling, IRONMAN, Swim with Jazz, Feisty Women's Performance, fuel/HQ, David Lloyd Clubs, Fast and Female, Team Picnic PostNL and the University of Chester; it does not say what each relationship is (slide 2).

detail.text: Why research leaned on men: the "70 kg male" became the reference participant; hormones were treated as noise; testing women properly means verifying phase with hormone measures across several phases; contraception variety makes uniform groups harder; product claims were built on male evidence, "This is where industry can now lead" (slide 5).

Women aren't one population: adolescents; menstruating women with a natural cycle; women on hormonal contraception, which suppresses endogenous hormones and may be used to manage conditions such as endometriosis; pregnancy and postpartum, a one to two year period; peri- and menopause, diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without menstruation. "Lots of individual variation across all phases" (slide 7). The hormone curves across the lifespan are marked "Illustrative – not to scale" (slide 8).

About 50% of elite athletes use hormonal contraception (Martin et al. 2018); 77% of non-users report negative cycle symptoms, mostly on days 1-2 of bleeding; peri- and postmenopausal athletes are almost absent from research; adolescents, pregnancy and postpartum have even less data; findings in one group can't simply be applied to another (slide 9).
She asked the room "Who is your target audience?" before the cycle-syncing section (slide 10). The cycle-syncing slide also shows an SiS Run Fuel gel and Fast and Female (slide 11).

Physiology: the 28-day cycle is an average, not a rule; the follicular phase is the more variable; the luteal phase lasts about 12-15 days after ovulation; the LH surge is not exactly day 14; stress, sleep, body weight, training load and life context all affect the pattern (slide 12). "Every woman will experience the menstrual cycle differently" (slide 13).

Proposed mechanisms. Muscle activation: in theory oestrogen raises excitability and progesterone "may lower strength outcomes in the luteal phase". Muscle and tendon stiffness: oestrogen may change collagen synthesis, but "Most research states this increase is not great enough to have an effect". Thermoregulation: a sufficient warm-up nulled any luteal advantage; higher body temperature could hurt endurance. Metabolism: trends disappear at higher intensities or when fed; exercise intensity and nutrition status appear "to be more influential than menstrual cycle phase" (slide 14).
One study found peak power higher in the ovulatory phase, but motivation to train was also greatest then; intermittent endurance is more likely to be affected than continuous endurance (slide 15).

What social media says (crossed out on the slide): train hard early, pilates and walking later. What the review says: performance "might be reduced by a small amount" in the early phase, with large personal differences (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 16). Her conclusion: a personalised approach based on each woman's response (slide 17).
Resting metabolic rate may rise slightly in the luteal phase, but studies are inconsistent and mostly low quality; combined pill users do not show these fluctuations (slide 18).

Protein: oestrogen is anabolic and progesterone catabolic, so in theory an athletic woman might need more protein in the luteal phase, but rising metabolic rate and appetite are already likely to raise her intake (slide 20).

The women's health aisle: UK menopause supplements projected to grow from £42m (2020) to £100m by 2028 (GenM/Kantar); Holland & Barrett women's health sales up 22% year on year; a UCL 2026 review found half of UK menopause supplements had no vitamin D and only 24% contained calcium; "hormone balance" stacks (DIM, inositol, vitex, ashwagandha) are booming online (slide 22).

Packs on the "Pink washing or progress?" slide, read from the pack shots: Wassen Prime Protect 50+ Women, Hairburst Womens 35+ Hair Vitamins (with added collagen), Viviscal, Swedish Collagen Collagen Deluxe (12,500 mg hydrolysed marine collagen), Novomins Women's Bio-Balance Gummies and Zooki Creatine+ for Women (slide 21).

The four rules in full: Justify (no trending "oestrogen balance" ingredients without evidence in active women); Dose and Disclose (no proprietary blends at token doses, untested for banned substances); Claim honestly (no "balances your hormones" or "cycle-synced" without trials; say what isn't yet known); Co-design (not "a pink tub on the same formula") (slide 23).

What industry can do: fund female-specific trials rather than adding women to male designs; verify menstrual status with best-practice methods, not day-counting; educate on who the product is for; research the product, not just the ingredient; publish null results (slide 24).

Take-home messages: more high-quality research across the lifespan; cycle effects small, individual variation large, energy availability first; products built on evidence; industry can fund, design and report better research (slide 25).

Her "Who am I?" slide carries logos including SiS, British Cycling, IRONMAN, Swim with Jazz, Feisty Women's Performance, fuel/HQ, David Lloyd Clubs, Fast and Female, Team Picnic PostNL and the University of Chester; it does not say what each relationship is (slide 2).

takeaways.text: The evidence gap: of 5,261 publications with 12,511,386 participants, 63% studied males and females, 31% males only and 6% females only (Cowley et al., 2021) (slide 4).

Even when women are included, 14% of performance supplement studies defined menstrual status and about 0.5% verified it with best-practice methods; female participation rose from about 39% (2011-13) to about 44% (2021-23) (Smith et al., 2022; Ose et al., 2025) (slide 6).

The cycle and performance: 13 of 16 studies found no effect on anaerobic performance and 14 of 22 none on aerobic performance; no influence of phase on strength or training adaptations, "BUT motivation could be impactful" (Carmichael et al., 2021; Colenso-Semple et al., 2023). A review found the evidence does not warrant general guidance on changing exercise across the cycle (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 15) (slide 16).

Nutrition: carbohydrate targets are per kg of body mass and apply to both sexes, with no evidence for phase-specific targets; energy intake tends to rise about 170 kcal a day in the luteal phase. The primary focus is adequate energy intake and optimal energy availability (ISSN position stand, Sims et al., 2023) (slide 18) (slide 19).

Protein: high-quality protein as close to the start and/or end of exercise as possible at 0.3-0.4 g/kg body weight, aiming for the upper end in the luteal phase "due to the catabolic actions of progesterone" (Sims et al., 2023) (slide 20).

Building better products: include only ingredients with evidence for the outcome claimed, "e.g. creatine 3–5 g/day alongside strength training for midlife muscle and strength"; use trial doses, list every dose, batch-test for athletes (e.g. Informed Sport); use authorised claims; co-design with women and fund female-specific studies (slide 23).

quotes.text: "Hormones treated as noise: the cycle was seen as a confounder to avoid rather than a variable to study." (slide 5)
"Carbohydrate needs are driven by the training session, not the cycle phase." (slide 18)
"Demand is outpacing evidence" (slide 22)
"Women's products should be built on evidence, not trends." (slide 25)

Talk to Emily Jevons (contact details on slides 1 and 26) about what a CreaWin study in active or midlife women should look like; she named creatine 3-5 g a day as her evidence-based example (slide 23).

Find the papers: Cowley et al. 2021, Smith et al. 2022, Ose et al. 2025, McNulty et al. 2020, Carmichael et al. 2021, Colenso-Semple et al. 2023, the ISSN female athlete position stand (Sims et al. 2023) and the UCL 2026 review of menopause supplements.
Find out who supplies the creatine in Zooki Creatine+ for Women and Marchon Women's Formula (slide 11) (slide 21).

Next up, and as next succinctly introduced this morning, we're going to explore how two key ingredients can work together to unlock new opportunities in performance and active nutrition, and to host our next presentation, whey collagen: the protein power couple. Please join me in welcoming to the stage Tess Plackett.

summary.Summary:
James Morton of Science in Sport asked whether women need to fuel differently from men when they run. His answer: the barrier is knowledge, not biology.

He started with glycogen. In a 2021 study of recreational runners, women began with less muscle glycogen than men but finished equally depleted. The gap came from dosing per kilogram of body weight: given the same absolute carbohydrate, women store about the same.

He then showed an England Athletics study of elite runners fed 60, 90 or 120 g of carbohydrate an hour over two hours near race pace. At 120 g the switch from carbohydrate to fat never came, in men or in women. Both sexes oxidised the extra carbohydrate equally well, and running economy improved by two to 3%. Women reported more gut symptoms, so tolerance may differ slightly, but oxidation does not.

From this he drew a framework that sets carbohydrate by intensity and duration, up to 120 g an hour for a marathon, and described SiS's partnership with Nike's After Dark Tour as an education programme rather than a product launch. His conclusion: female runners do not know the numbers and have lived with under-fuelling. Treat the female athlete as an athlete first, and fuel for the work, not the menstrual cycle.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished similarly depleted. The gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius, comes from dosing per kilogram, and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
- At 120 g of carbohydrate an hour, the crossover from carbohydrate to fat was completely prevented over two hours, in both sexes; at 60 g it came after about an hour [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Men and women oxidise carbohydrate taken during exercise at comparable rates, rising with dose (120 > 90 > 60 g); at 120 g some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took [00:00] (photo 7).
- Running economy improved by two to 3% at 120 g an hour, against the 4% Nike claimed for the Vaporfly; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00] (photo 9).
- Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; individual variation warrants personalised fuelling [00:00] (photo 9).
- The biggest barrier is educational, in a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent; he does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle [00:00] (photo 20).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Nothing in the talk touches our ingredients. No protein, creatine or pre-workout was mentioned from the stage; the only protein on a slide is 25 g (including 5 g collagen) in the two Run Recovery drinks of the Nike x SiS range, source not stated (photo 19).
- The value is customer insight. SiS builds its pitch on its own trials (England Athletics, Nike), published papers and a one-slide framework, and its chief science voice is openly sceptical of claims he sees on social media [00:00] (photo 12). My reading: a brand like this expects a supplier to bring trial data and a one-slide rule of thumb, not a benefit list; CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea material should meet that standard.
- Gut tolerance (more symptoms in women at high intakes, a runner skipping gels on an unhappy stomach) is adjacent to the digestibility story for a clear pea protein (photo 15) (my reading).
- The clear recovery drinks carry 25 g protein in a clear format for women runners, which is the format IsoClr: Pea is made for (photo 19) (my reading).
- Relevance low: carbohydrate fuelling, outside our range.

- "...for a given relative intake, then female participants may present with slightly less absolute glycogen. But if you ensure that they consume the same absolute amount of carbohydrate, then you don't really see any differences in glycogen storage." Speaker 1 (James Morton) [00:00]
- "...when we consume 120 grams of carbohydrate per hour, not only have you shifted the crossover point, you've completely prevented it." Speaker 1 (James Morton) [00:00]
- "...we get an improvement in running economy between two and 3%, depending on sexes, and so I'm I'm pretty sure that that's why you are seeing a lot of these running records and performances improve." Speaker 1 (James Morton) [00:00]
- "I would say that the biggest buyer to fueling the female runner is not biological. They don't have special guts or special muscles that we need to consider." Speaker 1 (James Morton) [00:00]

summary.Detail:
- The 2021 study (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise): recreational runners with muscle biopsies before and after three sessions, on 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m and 3 x 10 minutes [00:00].
- Given the same absolute carbohydrate, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage", even if women then take eight or nine grams per kilogram. His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].
- The elite study: men with marathon bests about 2:20, women about 2:40. 8 g per kg carbohydrate on day one, a 2 g per kg breakfast on day two, then 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint (simulated race pace) and 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold. The 60 g an hour condition was maltodextrin only; 90 and 120 g were 1:1 maltodextrin and fructose [00:00] (photo 2). The male data is Ravikanti et al. (2025), Journal of Applied Physiology; the female data is under revision [00:00].
- Crossover: at 60 g an hour, after about 60 minutes (the slides show about 60 to 75 minutes in both sexes); 90 g shifted it right; 120 g prevented it for the full two hours. Men's carbohydrate oxidation on 120 g held at about 3.0 to 3.2 g a minute from 45 to 105 minutes [00:00] (photo 3) (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported in literature". Peak means read from the chart: men about 1.0, 1.5 and 1.8 g a minute at 60, 90 and 120 g; women about 1.0, 1.45 and 1.75; seven to eight participants a group [00:00] (photo 7).
- The conclusion slide: "Female trained runners can oxidise exogenous CHO at comparable rates to male runners. Furthermore, in both sexes, 120 g/h maintains whole body CHO oxidation, CHO dependency and reduces the oxygen cost of running (i.e. improves running economy) compared with traditional CHO guidelines of 60-90 g/h. However, individual variations in rates of exogenous CHO oxidation and gastrointestinal symptoms warrant CHO personalisation strategies." (photo 9)
- Women may differ slightly in their ability to tolerate carbohydrate at those intensities; there is "definitely not a difference" in their ability to digest and oxidise it [00:00].
- The fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].
- The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 10) (photo 12).
- The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do), and tolerating carbohydrate in a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels). Like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Nike's After Dark Tour runs women's night races in seven cities. SiS partnered on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17) (photo 18).
- The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).
- The closing slide: "The biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles. Rather, it is lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines (i.e. educational) and the associated physiological and performance benefits, especially when considering a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent. Fuelling is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required." (photo 20) From the stage he added that he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling at all, and treats a female athlete as an athlete first [00:00].
- Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]. Women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure: "I'd rather be in the approximately right count than the precisely wrong count." [23:48] Dual source is needed at 90 and 120 g, above about 90 minutes, but not below, and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].

files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

James Morton presented research on carbohydrate metabolism, glycogen storage, and fueling strategies for runners.

## Glycogen Research
**James** discussed a 2021 study involving male and female recreational runners to examine muscle glycogen depletion in the *vastus lateralis* and *gastrocnemius* muscles.
* **Key Findings**: While females showed lower absolute resting glycogen stores, this was attributed to lower body mass and carbohydrate intake prescribed in grams per kilogram. When consuming the same absolute amount of carbohydrate, no significant differences in storage were observed.
* **Practical Implications**: The differences in glycogen concentration are trivial (less than five grams) and do not necessitate different nutritional guidelines for recreational runners.

## Fueling Strategies
**James** shared new, unpublished data regarding high-performance runners (marathon personal bests of 2:20 for men and 2:40 for women) to evaluate carbohydrate oxidation rates.
* **Oxidation Rates**: Consuming 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour prevented the "crossover effect" where the body shifts from carbohydrate to fat metabolism, maintaining carbohydrate dependency for the full two hours.
* **Running Economy**: Ingesting 120 grams per hour improved running economy by 2% to 3%, comparable to the impact of advanced footwear technology.
* **Fueling Matrix**: **James** proposed a strategy based on intensity and duration:
    1. Low intensity (<60 mins): No carbohydrate required.
    2. Moderate intensity (60 mins): 30–60 grams per hour.
    3. Long duration (Half marathon): Up to 90 grams per hour.
    4. Ultra-endurance (2–3+ hours): Target 120 grams per hour using dual-source blends (maltodextrin and fructose).

## Technical Discussion
During the Q&A, **Olivia** queried the methodology and specific nutrient types used in the studies.
* **Sample Size**: **James** confirmed that power analysis supported the sample size of nine participants due to the strong physiological effect observed when increasing doses by 30 grams per hour.
* **Nutrient Composition**: The 60g/hour dose utilized maltodextrin only, while 90g and 120g doses used dual-source maltodextrin and fructose to ensure gastrointestinal tolerance and maximize oxidation.
* **Open Questions**: Would prescribing carbohydrate in grams per kilogram of fat-free mass provide a more accurate dose for female athletes?

Women may differ slightly in their ability to tolerate carbohydrate at those intensities; there is "definitely not a difference" in their ability to digest and oxidise it [00:00].

The fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].

The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 10) (photo 12).

The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do), and tolerating carbohydrate in a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels). Like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).

Nike's After Dark Tour runs women's night races in seven cities. SiS partnered on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17) (photo 18).

The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).

The closing slide: "The biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles. Rather, it is lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines (i.e. educational) and the associated physiological and performance benefits, especially when considering a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent. Fuelling is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required." (photo 20) From the stage he added that he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling at all, and treats a female athlete as an athlete first [00:00].

Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]. Women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure: "I'd rather be in the approximately right count than the precisely wrong count." [23:48] Dual source is needed at 90 and 120 g, above about 90 minutes, but not below, and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].

takeaways.text: Women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished similarly depleted. The gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius, comes from dosing per kilogram, and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
At 120 g of carbohydrate an hour, the crossover from carbohydrate to fat was completely prevented over two hours, in both sexes; at 60 g it came after about an hour [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6).

Men and women oxidise carbohydrate taken during exercise at comparable rates, rising with dose (120 > 90 > 60 g); at 120 g some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took [00:00] (photo 7).
Running economy improved by two to 3% at 120 g an hour, against the 4% Nike claimed for the Vaporfly; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00] (photo 9).
Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; individual variation warrants personalised fuelling [00:00] (photo 9).
The biggest barrier is educational, in a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent; he does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle [00:00] (photo 20).

summary.Summary:
Tess Plaquet, technical sport manager at Rousselot, argued that brands should stop asking when whey prices will fall and work around them by blending whey with collagen.

She began with the market. Whey launches keep growing, and she said the forces behind whey prices, from GLP-1 users and China to whey being a cheese by-product and rising energy and labour costs, mean high prices are here to stay. Brands can raise prices, shrink packs or reformulate; she called smarter formulation with protein blends the most elegant answer. Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at 17.44% a year, and collagen comes from four animal sources with far steadier prices.

She then made the case that the two proteins complement rather than compete: whey builds and repairs muscle, while Rousselot's Peptan collagen peptides support tendons, joints and bone. Her evidence was Rousselot's own studies. The central one gave 22 men either 45 g of whey or 25 g of whey plus 20 g of Peptan for three weeks of training, and recovery and performance were similar in both groups. Studies of Peptan on its own reported less muscle soreness, fewer blood endotoxins after a run, better knee comfort and better sleep.

The recording ends as she invites the room to Rousselot's roundtables.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10] (slide 5).
- Launches combining whey and collagen grew at 17.44% a year from 2023 to 2026 to date, led by snacks, cereals and energy bars (39.7%) and nutritional and meal replacement drinks (36.4%); her example, Optimum Nutrition's clear whey isolate with collagen, has 10 g of each [00:10] (slide 6).
- Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
- Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10] (slide 8).
- In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey; the slide says such blends "may provide broader support across the musculoskeletal system" [00:10] (slide 9).
- 2 × 10 g Peptan a day with vitamin C, for a week before 150 drop jumps and two days after, gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo; the slide marks the soreness result as a likely benefit and the recovery result as significant [00:10] (slide 10).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Rousselot sells into the same brand problem we do, with a different answer: replace part of the whey with collagen, backed by a head-to-head showing no loss of recovery or performance at 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan [00:10]. My reading: IsoClr: Pea competes for the same "smarter formulation" slot in a brand's protein review, and our pitch should match hers in form: the supply argument first, then evidence that a blend performs.
- We have no head-to-head of this kind for pea; that is the gap (my reading).
- Her collagen supply story (four animal sources, little volatility) is the kind of supply-security argument a plant protein can make more strongly (my reading).
- Nick Morgan named whey plus collagen clear drinks earlier; a clear pea plus collagen format is a possible combination rather than a competition (my reading).
- The health claims here come from Rousselot's own studies, with her hedges; none are ours. Relevance high: protein blends and whey pricing.

- Endotoxins (Taylor et al., 2022): randomised, double-blind, cross-over; 20 men; 10 g Peptan or flavoured water for seven days, the last dose 45 minutes before a 70-minute run; endotoxins were the same as without exercise, while on placebo they rose. Her hedge: "...it's really an indication that taking in peptan could lessen the amount of endotoxins in your blood and could reduce your digestive discomfort" [00:10]. The slide: "Peptan could lessen the increase of blood endotoxin levels, a known cause of inflammation" (slide 11).
- Knees (Jiang et al., 2014): randomised, placebo-controlled; women with mild knee discomfort, 8 g a day for six months; joint discomfort (WOMAC) fell 10% at three months and 24% at six, and joint function (Lysholm) rose 4% and 7%, the chart marks each change p < 0.001 [00:10] (slide 12).
- Sleep (Thomas et al., 2023): randomised, double-blind, cross-over; 13 men; 15 g an hour before bed for seven days; polysomnography on night seven. The slide gives a 30% reduction in awakenings; on the chart they fell from about 30 to about 21, read from the chart, where she said "around 30 to 22, something like that". On the Stroop test the Peptan group scored about 1.00 against about 0.97 for control, read from the chart; she said the Peptan group "performed perfectly, 100%" [00:10] (slide 13).
- Rousselot offers roundtables on application advantages and help incorporating collagen [00:10] (slide 15).
- Slides after the close: Nextida GC, which Rousselot says was "specifically developed to target post-meal glucose spikes & boost GLP-1 secretion". Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (pilot 2024: 16 people, 5 g or 10 g; confirmation 2026: 30 people, 10 g; each taken 30 minutes before a carbohydrate-rich meal). Citing the 2026 study, for 10 g against placebo the slides give a 37% lower glucose spike, a 47% lower glucose peak, 82% more total GLP-1 exposure, a 53% higher GLP-1 response, a 70% higher GIP response and a lower post-meal insulin response. A 2026 Ipsos consumer study for Rousselot in the US (5 g twice a day for six weeks, N = 181) found 80% felt fuller for longer and 55% reported weight loss; the slide says this "does not constitute a consumer-facing claim" (slide 17) (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 21) (slide 22) (slide 23).

detail.text: Her deck arrived after the talk (files/rousselot-whey-collagen-deck.pdf, 23 pages). Slides 17 to 23 come after the closing "Thank you" slide and are not in the recording (see the last bullet).

Whey launches: food and beverage supplement launches featuring whey grew 7.53% a year from 2023 to 2025 (she said seven and a half percent), from about 18,600 in 2023 to about 19,800 in 2024 and 21,600 in 2025, read from the chart [00:10] (slide 3).

The "8.7" she gave as the biggest growth yet is, on the slide, the 2024 to 2025 rise of +8.73% in the average price of those launches: US$3.17 per 100 g in 2023, US$3.32 in 2024, US$3.61 in 2025 and US$3.78 in 2026 to date [00:10] (slide 3).

WPC80 price: she said "in 2023 the price of a ton of whey protein concentrate of 80% was 5.7 k, whereas in 2026 it's almost 32 k. So really, in just three years' time, it's almost a sixfold" [00:10]. The slide gives US$5.7k a tonne in June 2023 and US$31.7k in June 2026; the slide's sources are Mintel and Vesper, and it does not say which market the price is for (slide 3).

Another speaker's view of the same price: Alan Johnstone (Nutrilution, unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of) used Vesper's EU price in euros a kilogram: WPC80 about €5.2 in June 2023 and €27.4 in June 2026, read from his chart, and €27.00 in the week of 25 August 2026. Hers is in US dollars a tonne (US$5.70 and US$31.70 a kilogram). The two differ in currency and unit; both show close to a sixfold rise.

Her drivers, which she said mean "those prices will be here to stay": demand from active lifestyle consumers, GLP-1 users advised to take extra protein, and China; whey is a by-product of cheese and cannot be scaled easily; gas, electricity, labour, filtration costs, tariffs, geopolitics and climate push the same way [00:10]. The slide groups them as supply and demand imbalance, rising production and operational costs, and global economic and environmental factors, citing The Guardian, Rabobank, ScienceInsights and New Hope Network (slide 4).

Whey and collagen launches by year, read from the chart: about 320 in 2023, 320 in 2024, 420 in 2025 and 520 in 2026 to date. The chart's sources are Mintel, Holland & Barrett, ON, David and Rousselot (slide 6).

Whey is a complete protein rich in BCAAs, for muscle building and repair. Peptan is hydrolysed collagen, rich in hydroxyproline (unique to animal-derived collagen and, she said, linked to holistic health benefits), glycine and proline [00:10]. The slide adds that whey lacks hydroxyproline and Peptan lacks tryptophan (slide 8).

The head-to-head (Robberechts et al., 2023, IJSNEM): randomised, double-blind, parallel; 22 healthy, active men; 45 g whey against 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day; three weeks of training; jump height and creatine kinase measured; no difference between groups at the end [00:10] (slide 9).

Soreness (Clifford et al., 2019): 24 men, 2 × 10 g Peptan or maltodextrin placebo with vitamin C from day -7 to day 2, with doses 40 minutes before and straight after 150 drop jumps on day 0; soreness and muscle power at 48 hours. She described it as seven days of 20 g [00:10] (slide 10).

Endotoxins (Taylor et al., 2022): randomised, double-blind, cross-over; 20 men; 10 g Peptan or flavoured water for seven days, the last dose 45 minutes before a 70-minute run; endotoxins were the same as without exercise, while on placebo they rose. Her hedge: "...it's really an indication that taking in peptan could lessen the amount of endotoxins in your blood and could reduce your digestive discomfort" [00:10]. The slide: "Peptan could lessen the increase of blood endotoxin levels, a known cause of inflammation" (slide 11).

Knees (Jiang et al., 2014): randomised, placebo-controlled; women with mild knee discomfort, 8 g a day for six months; joint discomfort (WOMAC) fell 10% at three months and 24% at six, and joint function (Lysholm) rose 4% and 7%, the chart marks each change p < 0.001 [00:10] (slide 12).

Sleep (Thomas et al., 2023): randomised, double-blind, cross-over; 13 men; 15 g an hour before bed for seven days; polysomnography on night seven. The slide gives a 30% reduction in awakenings; on the chart they fell from about 30 to about 21, read from the chart, where she said "around 30 to 22, something like that". On the Stroop test the Peptan group scored about 1.00 against about 0.97 for control, read from the chart; she said the Peptan group "performed perfectly, 100%" [00:10] (slide 13).
Rousselot offers roundtables on application advantages and help incorporating collagen [00:10] (slide 15).

Slides after the close: Nextida GC, which Rousselot says was "specifically developed to target post-meal glucose spikes & boost GLP-1 secretion". Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (pilot 2024: 16 people, 5 g or 10 g; confirmation 2026: 30 people, 10 g; each taken 30 minutes before a carbohydrate-rich meal). Citing the 2026 study, for 10 g against placebo the slides give a 37% lower glucose spike, a 47% lower glucose peak, 82% more total GLP-1 exposure, a 53% higher GLP-1 response, a 70% higher GIP response and a lower post-meal insulin response. A 2026 Ipsos consumer study for Rousselot in the US (5 g twice a day for six weeks, N = 181) found 80% felt fuller for longer and 55% reported weight loss; the slide says this "does not constitute a consumer-facing claim" (slide 17) (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 21) (slide 22) (slide 23).

takeaways.text: Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10] (slide 5).

Launches combining whey and collagen grew at 17.44% a year from 2023 to 2026 to date, led by snacks, cereals and energy bars (39.7%) and nutritional and meal replacement drinks (36.4%); her example, Optimum Nutrition's clear whey isolate with collagen, has 10 g of each [00:10] (slide 6).
Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10] (slide 8).

In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey; the slide says such blends "may provide broader support across the musculoskeletal system" [00:10] (slide 9).

2 × 10 g Peptan a day with vitamin C, for a week before 150 drop jumps and two days after, gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo; the slide marks the soreness result as a likely benefit and the recovery result as significant [00:10] (slide 10).

"...there are more and more launches of products combining whey and collagen, so steady increase over the last couple of years, and yeah, actually an average growth rate of 17.5 percent almost." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
"...these two are no competitors; these two already complementary, and when you add in both, you can have extra additional health benefits." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
"So actually, the athletes, the recovery was the same, the performance was the same, but you also have more support in your movement system..." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]

# Built in the gym: Turning athlete insight into sports nutrition innovation: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Marchon - Fireside - SNS", https://otter.ai/u/pZI1Kf2nvFAS-7PcfNZZlCOVpH0, recorded 9 Nov 2026 12:05, 23m 1s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Olivia Haslam - NutraIngredients: Welcome to the stage the team behind March on Ollie Marchon, founder and Liam Bones, head of product. Okay, guys. Thank you so much for joining us. Okay, God, I've got a million questions for you. Where to start? Okay, so we've we we both heard, and we know this already, about how performance nutrition is no longer the domain of these elite athletes and kind of serious bodybuilders. It's much more broader, much more mainstream consumers. From your perspective, both of you, what has fundamentally changed in the way that people think about nutrition and performance, and what new demands has created the industry?
[00:54] Speaker 1 (Ollie Marchon): I'll go first. We've seen the rise of the every athlete. I think this has been born more prominently probably over the last five years. We've seen the running boom. We've seen the boom of high rocks. We've seen increase in people participating in strength. Now that's something that everyone's kind of engaging with. Someone just before mentioned the GLP-1. So I think those three categories: sort of running, evolving into functional fitness competitions, and striving to achieve things outside the gym, plus people in the gym now thinking about sets and reps and objectively measuring their strength. We've seen this this rise of the everyday athlete, and we categorize it into into into three. We've got the the inspired by every athlete that's looking to build those habits and routines, getting into the gym 345 times a week. They're looking for feeling based improvements, and I think our nutrition and supplementation goes towards how do we make someone feel better. So we're thinking about micronutrient deficiencies. We think about the given multivitamin, the omega, improving their sleep, and we'll always go from a food-first approach. But for these people, it's just about building those those incremental improvements through habits and routines. The driven buy is they're looking for objectively how can I measure my progress inside the gym and outside of it. They're they're worrying about their marathon time. They're worrying about their high rocks time. They're thinking about their their personal bests inside the gym, and for those people, we're thinking about nutrition strategies that might involve nutrient timing. summary.Summary:
Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients talked with Ollie Marchon, founder of the UK brand Marchon, and Liam Holmes, its head of product, about what the rise of the everyday athlete means for sports nutrition.

Ollie described three kinds of consumer: those inspired by training, who want habits and to feel better; those driven by it, who measure progress and time their nutrients; and those who live by it, planning the whole day around training. Most people on Marchon's training app train at 6 in the morning, which changes what they need. Liam argued for situational formats, such as carbohydrate in a pre-workout for people who cannot eat first.

Ollie said awareness of supplements is high but understanding lags, so education, honest positioning and effective doses matter more than hype. Creatine shows how this works: decades of research and podcast voices did the selling, and it built the daily supplement habit. Liam sees creatine as here to stay and moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers, the challenge is stability in water, gummies and other formats. Claims are a regulatory nightmare, so Marchon adds ingredients to products already in people's routines.

Asked where the category goes in five years, Liam answered: formats that improve compliance.

The founders of **Marchon** discussed the evolution of performance nutrition from an elite niche to a mainstream market driven by everyday athletes.

## Consumer Segments
**Ollie** and **Liam** identified three distinct consumer categories shaping the current industry landscape:
*   **Inspired Athletes**: Individuals focused on building habits and feeling better through micronutrients, sleep, and food-first approaches.
*   **Driven Athletes**: Goal-oriented consumers interested in objective metrics like marathon times or personal bests, requiring sophisticated nutrient timing strategies.
*   **Live-by Optimizers**: High-priority wellness seekers who view nutrition, recovery, and training as their central daily focus, often training early in the morning.

## Product Trends
The discussion highlighted shifts in how products are formulated and perceived by the modern consumer. 
**Liam** noted that while awareness of supplements like **creatine** is high due to influencers and longevity research, true scientific understanding still lags behind. **Ollie** emphasized "situational formulation," such as creating pre-workout fuels containing carbohydrates for those training at 5:00 AM or 6:00 AM when eating solid food is difficult. There is also a growing movement toward viewing gut health, immunity, and recovery as integral components of performance rather than just muscle growth.

## Industry Challenges
The speakers addressed several hurdles regarding compliance and scientific integrity:
*   **Education vs. Awareness**: Consumers often use products they see online without understanding efficacy or proper dosing, such as using electrolytes as a primary fuel source instead of carbohydrates. 
*   **Regulatory Compliance**: **Liam** mentioned the difficulty of communicating complex scientific benefits through marketing without violating regulations or oversimplifying claims.
*   **Future Innovation**: The team predicts that future growth will come from improved delivery formats—such as gummies, jellies, and ready-to-drink (RTD) options—designed specifically to increase user compliance and convenience.

How can brands effectively bridge the gap between high social media awareness and genuine consumer understanding to prevent "trend chasing"?

Liam on creatine: studied on strength, performance and muscle mass, now going into cognition and possibly recovery [08:24].

Opportunity areas: gut health, immunity, sleep and recovery, as people train harder, longer and across modalities. Gut health to absorb higher carbohydrate loads is "still something that's untapped" [09:36].

Discipline over hype: Ollie cited "2005" electrolyte brands launched last year (Otter's figure) and said marketing electrolytes as fuel in place of carbohydrate is "a bit of a miss"; low-sodium electrolytes to drink more water through the day are fine [11:15], [13:09].
Liam prefers established ingredients reaching new uses as research catches up (creatine for cognition, curcumin, certain probiotics) over "the new shiny ingredient" [14:05].
Claims: Marchon attaches ingredients to formats already in a routine, such as a creatine plus multivitamin or a "Brain Health Plus multivitamin" [15:23].
Many marathon runners a few weeks from their race had not tried a gel [16:50].
Dose matters: a magnesium product for sleep without the right amount gives no benefit, and disappointed first-time buyers move on to the next trend [18:39].

Compliance: Amazon now sets more hoops than TikTok Shop; YouTube channels, regulators and third-party lab testing are catching up with poor practice; Science in Sport's chief science officer and advisory boards are the model [20:29], [21:13].
Ingredient supply, prices and sourcing were not discussed; the only supplier point was the creatine format challenge [08:24] (my reading).

takeaways.text: Three segments of everyday athlete: "inspired by" (habits, feeling better, food first), "driven by" (measured progress, nutrient timing around training) and "live by" (optimisers who plan the whole 24 hours around training) [00:54].
Most of their 8,000 daily training-app users train at 6:00 in the morning, so Marchon put carbohydrate into a pre-workout for people who will not eat toast or porridge first [00:54], [04:00].
Awareness is high but understanding lags: gym-goers talk confidently about products they saw in an ad without knowing why, so "education is really critical at this stage" [05:29].
Liam: creatine is "here to stay" and the research is moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers the challenge is format, meaning stability in water, gummies and other formats [08:24].
When Marchon surveyed its gym members, the number one struggle was still hitting their daily protein requirement [16:50].
Five years out, Liam's bet is "formats that improve compliance": gummies, jellies, powders, RTDs, and convenience [22:11].
