Our next session considers how long Gavity Science translates into the relevant consumer outcomes. From strategic partner Holland and Barrett, please welcome Alex Glover. Probably best use one of those that's up there, I think.
[00:25] Speaker 2: Thank you. Yes, great. Everybody can hear me. So, hello, everyone. My name is Alex. So, I lead the product formulation team at Holden Barrack Global. I'm responsible for all of the own label products that Holden Barrett formulate and develop across the globe. And I'm really happy that you started out there saying is we are with you saying about deciding what to buy because that's really the information that we get as a retailer all the time, is why a customer is choosing to buy our products and it's how we communicate that the border of being scientifically led, a clinical outcome, and combining it with a customer outcome because customers don't speak clinical language, so that's the agenda, which we will skip over. So, there's a photograph of a tortoise on the screen, and I really like this this analogy because it was one of the first lectures I ever had doing my master's program. Was this exact image put up on the screen? So, why is there a tortoise on the screen? This is why there's a tortoise on the screen? A tortoise's biology fundamentally challenges the way we look at aging. A tortoise will live the majority of its life without any disability or ailment. As you compare to a human, we live approximately between 10 and 12 years with either a disability or poor health. So a tortoise fundamentally will challenge the notion that biology is we are destined to age in a poor way. I'm not saying we're all going to live to 200 years, but actually there is a biological plausibility that we can all age better. So it's not just smoke and mirrors. Lifespan to health. Nick touched on this very nicely in his talk about the difference between the two, and it's a really important distinction because I think the category should almost be renamed, not just longevity, because actually, we're not in the business of making people live longer; we're making them live better. How do we do that from a product perspective? So, we're in a very, very fortunate position where we have data of millions of consumers across the globe, and we can see what they're buying and how frequently they're buying it, which is obviously the most important thing that we all, as brand owners, want. Is we want customers not just to buy the product once, we want them to keep buying the product. So, I see a lot of this in the kind of cellular health space and the more novels products in the in the longevity spaces. They promise a lot from mechanism. It's all about sirtuins and parts and telomere lengths, and I think I was on a really interesting panel last week in London with our with our own customers. So we were talking to all of our customers. We had customers from all of our key groups, and we had customers from each of our key markets. And something that really stood out to me was the way that customers talk to us about our products. So we think we can communicate to the customer with the science and the claims, but the way customers talk to us. For example, there was there was a lady in one of our customer groups called Stay Healthies. These are customers around the 50 age group, and she was just saying, "Well, actually, all I want to be able to do is play with my grandchildren, get up out of my chair without making a noise, go on that hike, travel without being uncomfortable, and this is not something that we've seen in clinical literature about how can how can I play with my grandchildren, but actually it's how we translate scientific evidence to help consumers with their problems, and not just looking at what the science is saying. And this really does retain customers. So we see the biggest sales that in our own label portfolio is products that have a clear communicated benefit to joint function, joint comfort, brain function, etc. These things like this, not just focusing on disseminating the clinical literature. So yeah, they do not buy. So this is a really interesting point, and I had a bit of a debate with our science team about this one last week. Customers are not buying into the mechanism. They are buying your product based off how they feel and how they continue to feel taking your product. So, common questions that we get as a retailer all the time is when timescale. When am I going to feel a benefit? What kind of benefit am I going to feel taking the product? And that's when we look to lean on the science because we can say, well, the population we saw a benefit within four weeks, within eight weeks, within six weeks, and with a strong scientific communication strategy that we have as a brand, we can sometimes communicate those things to the customer on pack. Can I measure it? Do I feel an improvement? Can I walk without pain? Can I play longer with my grandchild? Can I walk a little bit longer? Can I travel in more comfort? These are some of the really common ones that we get. And how much is it going to cost? I think Nick's slide said it really well. I think was it one euro 36 or something? And actually, some of the most cost effective evidence based interventions to improve longevity are nutritional interventions. Things like fiber, vitamin D, calcium, protein. All of these things have a really high level of evidence compared to some other newer, more novel technologies, and they're really cost-effective. Vitamin D, I think, costs about two cents per 10 microgram serving. I worked out from our from our own label. Most of our customers are not asking or saying, "What's my NAD level? How long are my telomeres? Are my siruin scavenging free radicals, or how active are my parts? I have never once heard any of those things from our customers. It's not to say they don't matter. The evidence gap. So when I'm talking to ingredient ingredient suppliers all the time, and I'm very immersed in clinical research, and a lot of the time, I'm seeing ingredients and the industry getting stuck in the first two blue sections of this. We're very focused on mechanism. We're very focused on biomarkers, but we're not focused on not just the clinical outcome, the customer outcome. What does the customer want? So, for example, if we take sleep, you know, I had a an ingredient the other day I was reading about, and they were constantly talking about the Pittsburgh Sleep Inventory, and I was like, a customer is not going to understand that. A customer wants to know, am I going to sleep better? Am I going to wake up feeling more refreshed? So a little bit of a case study because it's a very hot topic in our business at the moment is NAD and NAD boosters. So, what do we know about NAD? I won't bore you with the research, but I think the most important thing I will take is a customer case study. Again, is we presented some concepts around cellular health and cellular aging to a group of customers about a month ago, and the feedback was absolutely fascinating because I'd never actually heard the customer, how the customers perceive NAD and cellular health. Not a single customer knew what NAD was. There was over 1000 people that we surveyed. Not a single one knew what NAD was. And when we surveyed, what do you think cellular health is as a concept? And actually, from my perspective as a nutrition scientist, when I look at the research for nicotinamide riboside, nicotinamide mononucleotide, the outcome level data, if I think back to that last slide, is very very limited, especially when we compare it. I'm not sure if this is the right slide because there should be a nutrition. Okay, this is not the right slide, so I will. That's fine. Let me go back to this one. So the. yeah, the outcome-based data. One of the trials here is actually from a 2026 April this year metro analysis that looked at nicotinamide riboside, but it specifically looked at NAD boosting and outcomes. summary.Summary:
Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett's Global Product Formulation Lead, runs the team that formulates its own-label products worldwide. He asked how longevity science becomes something a customer will buy. His answer: consumers may buy a story, but they judge a product on the outcomes they feel.

He opened with a tortoise to argue that ageing badly is not biologically fixed, so the category is about living better, not longer. H&B's data on millions of customers show that repeat purchase goes to products with one clearly communicated benefit, such as joint function or brain function. Shoppers ask when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs. His slides set the test an ingredient must pass: evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance.

Two case studies followed. NAD boosters have a strong molecular rationale but very limited functional outcome data, and of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was. Curcumin, H&B's second best-selling ingredient, shows the other path: a meta-analysis of 11 trials found it improved knee osteoarthritis pain scores. He also named cheap basics with strong evidence: fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein.

His conclusion for suppliers: bring ingredients with both a biological rationale and human outcome data, and help retailers translate the science without over-promising.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Mechanisms make promises and sell, but outcomes retain customers (slide 6). Shoppers ask whether and when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs (slide 8); when trials show a benefit at four, six or eight weeks, H&B can sometimes put that on pack [00:25].
- H&B's test for an ingredient has five parts: evidence (high-quality science), dose (the effective, studied dose), outcome (which endpoint improves), communication (legal and responsible) and consumer relevance (does it matter in everyday life) (slide 6).
- The outcomes consumers buy are energy, memory, strength, mobility, sleep, appearance and feeling younger or better, not NAD+, sirtuins, telomeres or PARPs (slide 8). H&B's biggest own-label sellers carry one clear benefit, such as joint function, joint comfort or brain function [00:25].
- NAD: of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was [00:25]. NR reliably raises blood NAD metabolites and NMN or NAM raise it in some studies, but functional outcome improvements are "very limited" (slide 13).
- Curcumin is the "tangible outcomes" case: a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (n=1258) found curcuminoids improved VAS and WOMAC pain scores in knee osteoarthritis against comparators or placebo, and formulation matters because bioavailability varies widely (slide 15).
- Cheap interventions with strong evidence (fibre, vitamin D, calcium, protein) beat novel technologies on evidence and cost; US shelves are "protein plus fiber" [00:25]. None of this is on his slides.
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance stays medium: a major retailer's test for ingredients, adjacent to our range; the slides name none of our ingredients.
- The formulation lead at one of our customers' biggest retailers checks evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance (slide 6), and wants ingredients with "both biological rationale and human outcome" data (slide 17). My reading: CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea dossiers for retail-led brands should lead with the studied dose, the endpoint that improves and when the user feels it, before any mechanism.
- Strength and mobility are two of the seven outcomes he says consumers buy (slide 8). My reading: a healthy-ageing pitch for CreaWin and pea protein should speak of strength and getting out of a chair, not muscle protein synthesis.
- "Everything is protein plus fiber" in the US, and protein is among his cheap, evidence-rich longevity interventions [00:25]. My reading: pea protein with fibre is a brief European brands will copy, and IsoClr: Pea's taste and clarity are the arguments inside that blend.
summary.Quotes:
- "Customers are not buying into the mechanism. They are buying your product based off how they feel and how they continue to feel taking your product." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
- "Not a single customer knew what NAD was. There was over 1000 people that we surveyed." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
- "I'm sure if anybody's been to the US in the last six months, everything is protein plus fiber." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
- "Longevity science is rich in mechanisms, but consumers experience outcomes." (slide 17)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Alex Glover which endpoints, timescales and doses H&B accepts on pack for protein and creatine, measured against his five tests.
- Confirm which paper he meant by the April 2026 meta-analysis; his slide shows the October 2025 Nature Metabolism review.
- Question: how H&B's own-label sports and active nutrition ranges are sourced, and whether Alex's team formulates them.
- Nick's talk, referenced for lifespan against healthspan and a cost-per-day figure, is filed as nick-morgan-longevity.

Alex Glover discusses the necessity of translating complex scientific mechanisms into tangible consumer outcomes to drive product sales and customer retention.

## Consumer Insights
**Translating Science**
**Alex** emphasizes that while researchers focus on biological mechanisms like sirtuins, telomeres, or **NAD**, consumers prioritize functional benefits. Customers do not use clinical language; they want to know if a product will help them play with grandchildren, walk without pain, or sleep more refreshingly. **Alex** notes that the highest sales in the **Holland & Barrett** own-label portfolio come from products with clearly communicated benefits for joint function, brain function, and comfort.

**Market Realities**
**Alex** highlights a significant gap in consumer understanding regarding longevity science. In a survey of over 1,000 people, not a single respondent knew what **NAD** was. While there is high interest in "cellular health," consumer definitions are vague, covering everything from fertility to immunity. This suggests that marketing novel ingredients requires bridging the gap between clinical biomarkers and everyday feelings.

## Product Strategy
**Evidence Based Interventions**
**Alex** argues that cost-effective, traditional nutritional interventions often have stronger evidence bases than newer technologies. Examples include:
* **Fiber**: Reduces coronary heart disease risk by approximately 9% per seven grams of intake.
* **Vitamin D**: Highly cost-effective, costing roughly two cents per 10 microgram serving.
* **Curcumin**: A top-selling ingredient globally (one bottle sold per minute) that supports joint flexibility and reduces systemic inflammation.

**The Longevity Gap**
The discussion contrasts the "longevity" category—which implies living longer—with the goal of helping people "live better." **Alex** points out that many industry players get stuck in the "blue sections" of research, focusing on mechanisms and biomarkers rather than clinical outcomes. The primary questions from retailers and customers remain: "When am I going to feel a benefit?" and "How much is it going to cost?"

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

**Two Waves** is a digital platform designed to streamline the manufacturing ecosystem between brands, manufacturers, and ingredient suppliers.

## Market Challenges
The manufacturing market is projected by **Grandview Research** to grow at over 12 percent annually, exceeding $60 billion by 2030. However, current processes suffer from significant inefficiencies:
* Lack of visibility in specific product categories.
* Incomplete inquiries and fragmented communication across multiple email threads.
* High operational costs due to wasted time organizing data and searching for agreements.
* Lost opportunities resulting from missed offers or inquiries that do not reach the right partners.

## Platform Solutions
**Viktor** and **Matthew** introduced **Two Waves** as a tool to centralize quoting and negotiation through several key modules:
* **New Partnerships**: Instead of one-to-one outreach, one inquiry automatically reaches all verified manufacturers within a specific category, allowing for rapid comparison of structured offers.
* **Standardized Quoting**: The platform uses structured templates tailored to product categories to eliminate "communication noise" and ensure all key information is present.
* **Negotiation Management**: Users can manage quoting variants and track the full history of negotiations in a single location. 
* **Feedback Loops**: If an inquiry or offer is declined, the system provides a specific reason to improve future interactions.

## Security Infrastructure
**Matthew** addressed the risks associated with traditional communication methods like phone calls and emails, where data control is easily lost once information enters an inbox. To mitigate these risks, **Two Waves** implements:
* Mandatory company verification for all users to ensure participants are interacting only with verified entities.
* Enhanced control over how sensitive information is shared during the initial stages of business relationships.

summary.Summary:
The day's closing panel brought together a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina Pavlová, FAVEA), an ingredient company (Matts Johansen, chief executive of Aker BioMarine), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra). The moderator asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI.

They agreed that the consumer comes first. Alexandra wanted evidence-based claims and better communication, Martina a focus on what consumers actually need, and Alex a few claims done well, starting from the consumer's problem rather than piling on ingredients. Matts wanted a revolution in clinical trials: high-dose studies in people with real problems, published where consumers' chatbots will find them.

On regulation they differed in tone. Joanna wants food law to be a shield for innovators, though the claims system was written for vitamins. Matts was blunter: a three-year longer approval in Europe than in the US almost makes innovation impossible.

On supply, Matts warned of a fish oil shortage reaching shelves next summer. Alex described pre-bought stock and protecting the claim shoppers buy. Joanna said blaming the supplier is no defence.

On AI they wanted a human in the loop and peer-reviewed sources, and Matts warned that anyone who cannot use AI will not be able to work in two years.

The panel discussed the evolving landscape of the nutraceutical industry, focusing on scientific evidence, regulatory challenges, and technological integration.

## Industry Trends
**Alexandra**, **Matt**, and **Alex** highlighted the increasing demand for evidence-based products and high-quality communication.
*   **Alexandra** emphasized that consumers are increasingly well-informed but often rely on unqualified sources, necessitating better communication of factual ingredient claims.
*   **Matt** suggested a revolution in clinical trials, advocating for high-dose studies on individuals with actual health problems rather than healthy subjects to generate more meaningful data.
*   **Alex** noted that consumers prioritize solving specific problems and prefer clear, specialized messaging over brands that attempt to market too many ingredients or claims simultaneously.

## Regulatory Challenges
**Joanna** and **Martina** addressed the friction between innovation and legal frameworks.
*   **Joanna** explained that current food laws were designed for common ingredients like vitamin C and D, making it difficult for innovators to use clinical trial data to support new claims. She urged R&D teams to involve lawyers early in the development process to ensure compliance is a "shield" rather than a "heartbreak."
*   **Martina** observed that legislation often acts as an obstacle for CDMOs and advised businesses not to simply chase every market gap but to focus on deep understanding and consumer needs.
*   **Matt** raised concerns regarding the speed of European regulations compared to the **U.S.**, noting that a three-year delay in approval can make the net present value of new ingredients economically unviable.

## Supply and Technology
The discussion concluded with the impact of supply chain volatility and artificial intelligence.
*   **Matt** warned of a looming collapse in the fish oil supply chain due to aquaculture industry competition and potential traceability issues involving illegal fishing. 
*   **Alex** noted that retailers must proactively manage lead times and prepare for price increases or shifts in consumer preference if core ingredients like omega-3 become unavailable.
*   **Joanna** and **Alexandra** discussed the role of **AI**, noting its utility in searching peer-reviewed databases and managing factory sensors. **Joanna** stressed the importance of keeping a "human in the loop" to maintain legal integrity and trust, while **Matt** predicted that proficiency in operating **AI** tools will become a mandatory job requirement within two years.

summary.Summary:
Marit Weinstra of HMT, the Healthy Marketing Team, a food and health branding and innovation agency, opened the probiotic programme. Her question was how to win in a biotics market that has grown into a jungle of products. Use keeps rising, yet in seven of eight European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics.

She traced four eras. Yakult made good bacteria a daily ritual. Activia made the benefit tangible, and brands began competing on CFU counts. Then survival technology became the story. Now the shift is from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut barrier as the gateway to the rest of the body.

From that she drew four rules: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the ecosystem, benefits consumers can measure and feel, and everyday food formats. Her examples were mostly American: Pendulum's Akkermansia products for metabolic health, a prebiotic fibre brand, a digestive brand that sets expectations week by week, and Poppi.

Her conclusion: in Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand has to carry them. Value is moving from what is inside the product to what the consumer gets. A strong probiotic needs a "Double IP": the science and the brand.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Biotics have never been more popular: probiotic use among US adults rose 287% from 2009 to 2023, and European online probiotic sales have grown 15-25% a year since 2020 (slide 2). Yet in 7 of 8 European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics (slide 6); she said this without figures [00:24].
- Rule 1, from "more is better" to quality and proof: a number on its own no longer builds trust, so be an expert brand in a niche (slide 14). Shelves show 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU [03:59]; her niche example is Pendulum, an Akkermansia-based US brand for metabolic health (slide 14) [03:59].
- Rule 2, from adding bacteria to feeding the ecosystem: "eat more plants" instead of strain names, plants and fibre consumers can see, and a gut they feed themselves (slide 15); fibre brands lead this language [03:59].
- Rule 3, from belief to measurable and felt benefits: early adopters measure with microbiome tests, apps and personal scores; the mass market wants less bloating, regularity and energy, and buys again only if it notices a difference (slide 16). Her example sets expectations at week 1 and months 1, 2 and 3 (slide 17); she said "for one week, for one month" [03:59].

Marit Weinstra from **HMT** discusses the evolution of the probiotic market and shifting consumer expectations toward holistic gut health.

## Market Evolution
The probiotic category has moved through several distinct eras, transitioning from basic awareness to complex ecosystem management.
*   **First Era**: Focused on the concept of "good" vs "bad" bacteria, popularized by **Yakult** as a daily ritual.
*   **Second Era**: Led by **Danone Activia**, which focused on making intangible benefits like digestion more tangible via branding.
*   **Third Era**: Centered on technology and survival, where the primary promise was ensuring bacteria arrive alive in the gut.
*   **Current Era**: Shifting from simply adding bacteria to nourishing the entire gut ecosystem, focusing on terms like the gut barrier and fermentation.

## Strategic Shifts
To succeed in the current "jungle" of products, brands must follow four new industry rules to build consumer trust and clarity.
*   **Quality over Quantity**: Moving away from competing solely on high CFU counts (e.g., 50 billion or 100 billion) toward proven, niche expertise such as metabolic health.
*   **Ecosystem Nourishment**: Transitioning from adding single strains to providing plant diversity and fibers that proactively feed existing gut flora.
*   **Measurable Benefits**: Shifting from invisible promises to felt or measured results, utilizing microbiome tests or apps for early adopters while ensuring mass-market consumers feel immediate physical differences.
*   **Consumer-Centric Formats**: Moving from functional supplements toward desirable everyday food formats, similar to how **Poppi** approaches the category.

## Branding Strategy
Because many health claims are restricted in Europe compared to the U.S., brands must rely on emotional value rather than just rational science. 
*   Building a "double IP" involves combining rational scientific evidence with an emotional brand identity to ensure long-term protection and market presence. 
*   Success requires turning scientific innovation into a consumer-centric value proposition that provides clarity amidst excessive market options.

Novonesis and Montepharmaco discussed the importance of science-backed partnerships in developing successful probiotic consumer products.

## Company Profiles
**Ariel Annoni** introduced **Novonesis**, a company formed by the combination of **Novozyme** and **Chr. Hansen**, bringing over 100 years of expertise in biotechnology and microorganisms. The company focuses on providing probiotics, postbiotics, enzymes, vitamins, and HMOs to help brands differentiate themselves through scientific credibility and quality.

**Alessia** presented **Montepharmaco**, an Italian pharmaceutical company founded in 1945. Their brand **Lactoflorene** is a leading probiotic line in Italy, focusing on gut health for various demographics, including children and those with IBS.

## Strategic Partnership
The collaboration between **Novonesis** and **Montepharmaco** began in the early 2000s to address specific regulatory challenges in Italy regarding potency and stability.

**Key partnership achievements include:**
* Meeting Italian regulatory requirements by ensuring at least 1 billion colony-forming units (CFU) per product.
* Developing the **MCAP system**, a specialized delivery solution for liquid shots and food supplements.
* Conducting clinical studies on finished products to go beyond standard regulatory demands.
* Maintaining a core formula that has remained essentially unchanged for nearly 20 years.

## Market Success
The partnership has resulted in significant commercial growth for the **Lactoflorene** brand within the European market.

**Market performance metrics:**
* **Lactoflorene** currently holds approximately a 7% market share in Italy.
* The brand is ranked third in the Italian probiotic market.
* Growth is driven by clinical evidence, innovative delivery formats, and catering to diverse consumer needs across different age groups.

**Ariel Annoni** concluded that success in the probiotic sector requires more than just high-quality ingredients; it necessitates long-term partnerships involving formulation expertise, consumer insight, and scientific documentation.

Sacco System's speaker presented the company as a family-owned probiotic maker and CDMO that sells speed and flexibility. The recording joins mid-introduction, and the slides do not name him. Sacco dates from 1872 and turned over €195 million in 2025.

He described its offer: probiotics, postbiotics and tailor-made mixtures, strains screened to EFSA safety requirements, custom fermentation at any scale, and next-generation strains developed for third parties. Sacco has recently invested in clinical studies and patents in two areas, women's health and healthy ageing, and he gave one strain for each.

CA15, a patented strain isolated from a healthy woman, was tested in two placebo-controlled trials in women with vaginal imbalance. He reported fewer symptoms after ten days, held a month after intake stopped.

Synbio, a patented mix of two strains isolated from elderly people in Marche, was tested over six months in 97 healthy people over 65. He reported more beneficial bacteria and butyrate, a 43% fall in a marker of inflammation, higher IGF-1, which he linked to muscle maintenance, and slower shortening of telomeres.

His close was an invitation: Sacco will take on unusual projects quickly and work closely with the customer.

- CA15 results: symptom scores fell 78% for discomfort, 66% burning, 64% itching, 62% secretions and 56% inflammation (slide 15). On the Amsel criteria 98% of women had a corrected pH, 92% a negative amine test, 79% no clue cells and 75% normal discharge, as labelled on the chart (slide 16); he gave the first three the same [00:00].
- Synbio trial: L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502, 5 billion CFU a serving for six months in 97 healthy people over 65, randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled (slide 21) (slide 23); spoken as "five mil" daily [00:00].
- Synbio results, end of study against start: hs-CRP down 43%, IL-8 down 83%, IL-6 67%, MIP-1α 60% and TNF-α 23% (slide 25); total short-chain fatty acids up 23% and butyric acid up 33% (slide 26) [00:00].

The meeting presents the capabilities and patented probiotic solutions of **Sacco**, a family-owned CDMO specializing in pharmaceutical and food-grade active ingredients.

## Company Overview
**Sacco** is an agile, family-owned company with global operations including manufacturing plants in Italy (Como and Milan) and the US (Wisconsin). Their infrastructure supports various production needs:
*   **CSL** (Milan): Specialized in pharmaceutical API probiotics.
*   **Sacosystem Australia** (Brisbane): A pilot facility focused on next-generation bacteria, exotic strains, and LVPs.
*   **Quality Standards**: They offer both GMP pharma-standard facilities for high-end APIs and conventional GMP food-grade sites, supported by validation experts.
*   **Services**: Capabilities include providing probiotics, postbiotics, customized mixtures, and a "made-for-you" service for third-party strain development.

## Product Portfolio
The presentation highlights two primary areas of investment: women's health and healthy aging.

**Women's Health: CA15**
**CA15** is a patented strain isolated from vaginal samples in 2022. 
*   **Efficacy**: Clinical studies involving 200 women showed significant reduction in symptoms of bacterial vaginosis and vaginal candidiasis, such as burning, itching, and inflammation.
*   **Diagnostic Results**: Post-treatment (10 days) and one month after washout, 98% of subjects showed restored pH ranges and 92% had negative amine tests.
*   **Mechanism**: The strain survives gastrointestinal transit, colonizes the vagina, promotes natural lactobacilli like *G. acidophilus*, and reduces pathogens like *Gardnerella vaginalis*.

**Healthy Aging: Symbio**
**Symbio** is a synergistic mixture of *L. paracasi* and *L. rhamnosus* isolated from the Italian Marche region.
*   **Clinical Findings**: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 97 subjects over six months, **Symbio** increased gut microbiota diversity (Akkermansia, Bifidobacteria) and short-chain fatty acids like butyrate.
*   **Inflammation & Muscle Mass**: Results showed a 43% reduction in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and improved insulin growth factor one levels to combat sarcopenia.
*   **Longevity**: Blood analysis indicated a decrease in the rate of telomere shortening, a key marker of biological aging.

summary.Summary:
Two suppliers shared this slot. Miguel of SPI Pharma, an ABF Ingredients company, presented "From platform to product". His case: consumers buy formats first, so the gap is not another active but a format people will take. Last year SPI Pharma showed probiotics can be tableted. This year it showed what that tablet becomes.

He showed three concepts, each on an SPI platform. A mint chewable probiotic for adults, pressed gently on a low-moisture platform so the cultures survive. A fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport, kept stable by a modified sodium bicarbonate; a light fizz also masks bitterness. A vanilla fast-melt for healthy ageing that needs no water. The packs were illustrative concepts. His close: do not ask the consumer to swallow another capsule. The deck also asked the room for ideas, as SPI Pharma looks to grow in nutrition.

Mihail Jakubowski of Nordic Biotic then presented a supplier of clinically tested probiotic strains, sold with exclusivity by territory. He showed a stress and sleep blend tested on 227 students at exam time, saying the results, received the week before, proved efficacy on sleep quality and stress. He also showed a blend aimed at microplastics, with its human study still in progress. He closed with an invitation to develop products together.

- Chewable probiotic: Compressol ProTab is a low water activity direct-compression platform that compresses at low force, so live cultures survive; the concept is an adult mint chew, "Gut Performance Chew" (slide 5) (slide 7) [00:01].
- Effer-Soda is a surface-modified sodium bicarbonate, stable across packing forms, "not only desiccant tubes": 15–25% of a tablet or sachet formula as the effervescent system, or 1–4% for sparkle in a chewable or fast-melt; the concept is a fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport (slide 8) (slide 10) [00:01].
- Fast-melt: Advantol 300 with Effer-Soda 12 disintegrates in under 10 seconds, 20–40% faster than typical direct-compression competitors, and uses standard packaging, not lyophilised blisters (slide 14) (slide 15). It is aimed at children and older people who cannot or will not swallow [00:01].
- Nordic Biotic: full exclusivity by territory at strain level; genomics, then metabolomics (630 molecules, "the postbiotics actually"), then functional testing, then human studies [09:25].
- Mental Balance: eight-week study, 227 students started, 219 completed, "one of the largest study in stress in probiotics in the last decade"; results received last week; he said statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress [09:25].
- Nordic Biotic has a GLP-1 companion product with its Swiss sister company Azento [09:25].

- Medium relevance, unchanged by the deck: formats, not ingredients. The deck names no creatine or protein. Its sport concept, a fizzy electrolyte and caffeine stick made for athletes, is the kind of format our sports customers sell, and SPI Pharma's platforms are what a CDMO uses to make it.

A fast-melt suits small doses better than a gram-level creatine serving, so the chew and the stick are the likelier fits. Favea, shown making a live chewable, is a CDMO to know.

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

The meeting focused on innovative probiotic dosage forms and clinically tested probiotic strain technologies.

## Dosage Form Innovation
**Miguel** from **SPI Pharma** presented advanced delivery systems designed to improve consumer experience and stability.
*   **Composol Pro Tab**: A polyol-based, low water activity platform used to create chewable probiotic tablets with low compression forces to ensure probiotic survival.
*   **Effer Soda**: A partially transformed sodium bicarbonate product that creates a protective layer, enhancing stability in effervescent tablets, stick packs, or sachets. This technology can also produce a "delicate fizz" in fast-melting solutions to mask bitterness.
*   **Orally Disintegrating Tablets (ODT)**: Fast-melting platforms designed for populations with dysphagia, such as children and the elderly, allowing for consumption without water.

## Probiotic Research
**Mihail Jakubowski** of **Nordic Biotic** detailed scientific advancements in specialized probiotic strains and their metabolic functions.
*   **Northbiotic Mental Balance**: Developed with the **Polish Academy of Sciences**, this blend uses **Lactobacillus plantarum 140** (producing GABA) and **Bifidobacterium breve 010** (producing vitamin B free). An eight-week study of 227 students demonstrated statistical efficacy in improving sleep quality and managing stress.
*   **Microplastic Management**: A novel approach using two specific strains for gut cleansing:
    1.  **Lactobacillus acidophilus 120**: Aggregates and binds microplastic particles.
    2.  **Lactobacillus fermentum 160**: Pushes microplastics away from the mucosal lining to facilitate removal.
*   Human studies regarding the microplastic-binding technology are currently in progress.

## Strategic Partnerships
Both speakers emphasized opportunities for collaborative development between manufacturers and researchers. 
*   **Miguel** invited participants to use **SPI Pharma's** concept-driven approach to expand existing portfolios into new dosage forms like hydration sticks or chewable probiotics. 
*   **Mihail Jakubowski** proposed the **Plastic Gut-Free Initiative**, inviting brand owners and CDMOs to participate in co-development projects centered on microbiome research and genomics.

Action items: none returned.

The chewable was also shown as a live product at the SPI Pharma stand under Favea's branding; Martina had it [00:01]. The deck does not name Favea.

SPI Pharma's role, as he put it, is creating product concepts so a CDMO can expand into new dosage forms; "we do not limit there" [00:01]. The deck: "Bring the active. We bring the delivery system." (slide 15)

The deck says SPI Pharma "is looking to expand in the nutra market and would appreciate input from Remedy". It asks which trends and dosage forms need new excipient solutions, and whether a fully formulated delivery system would interest the room (slide 16).
His close is worded slightly differently on the slide: "Do not ask the consumer to swallow another capsule." (slide 17) [07:50]
Nordic Biotic, a silver sponsor, supplies clinically tested probiotics to brand owners, CDMOs and distributors; CFU is measured to milligrams [09:25].

Mental Balance (Northbiotic Mental Balance): strains chosen for what they produce, Lactobacillus plantarum 140 (GABA) and Bifidobacterium breve 010 (a B vitamin); tested in students at exam time [09:25].

Microplastic blend: Lactobacillus acidophilus 120 aggregates (binds) microplastic, Lactobacillus fermentum 160 pushes it away; offered as a standalone or an add-on to a gut, detox or clean-label formula; human study in progress, with an invitation to a "plastic gut-free initiative" [09:25].
Gut-skin, gut-bone and gut-brain technologies were named [09:25].
WIPO innovation index as he cited it: of 12 countries, seven are European; in the region Latvia, Czechia, Hungary and Poland lead [09:25].
His closing line: "We will not proudly invent the the next wheel in the next week, but I'm pretty sure we can create something new together." [09:25]
The chair's aside: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicinal tonic for brain and nerves [08:30].

takeaways.text: Chewable probiotic: Compressol ProTab is a low water activity direct-compression platform that compresses at low force, so live cultures survive; the concept is an adult mint chew, "Gut Performance Chew" (slide 5) (slide 7) [00:01].

Effer-Soda is a surface-modified sodium bicarbonate, stable across packing forms, "not only desiccant tubes": 15–25% of a tablet or sachet formula as the effervescent system, or 1–4% for sparkle in a chewable or fast-melt; the concept is a fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport (slide 8) (slide 10) [00:01].

Fast-melt: Advantol 300 with Effer-Soda 12 disintegrates in under 10 seconds, 20–40% faster than typical direct-compression competitors, and uses standard packaging, not lyophilised blisters (slide 14) (slide 15). It is aimed at children and older people who cannot or will not swallow [00:01].
Nordic Biotic: full exclusivity by territory at strain level; genomics, then metabolomics (630 molecules, "the postbiotics actually"), then functional testing, then human studies [09:25].

Mental Balance: eight-week study, 227 students started, 219 completed, "one of the largest study in stress in probiotics in the last decade"; results received last week; he said statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress [09:25].
Nordic Biotic has a GLP-1 companion product with its Swiss sister company Azento [09:25].

quotes.text: "The gap is not another strain. It is a chewable adults will actually take." SPI Pharma deck (slide 5)

"We received the results last week, so I just want to tell you that we have proved the statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress." Speaker 4 (Mihail Jakubowski, Nordic Biotic) [09:25]

followups: Confirm the SPI Pharma speaker's full name and role; the deck does not name him. Martina (SPI Pharma, at the stand) showed the Favea chewable [00:01].
Ask SPI Pharma whether Compressol ProTab or Effer-Soda 12 can carry a gram-level creatine dose in a chew or stick, and request samples (slide 17).
Confirm Mihail Jakubowski's name spelling and role at Nordic Biotic; the contact he gave was heard as "helloartnordibiotic.com" [09:25].
Ask Nordic Biotic for the Mental Balance student study when published and for the Azento GLP-1 companion product details [09:25].
Which CDMOs in the room use SPI Pharma's platforms for sports formats (sticks, effervescents, chewables)? Ask Favea.
